# Appendix DG - Printed servo-to-Lego coupler STL generated and validated; no cheaper commercial source exists; no torque margin claimed (2026-09-03 23:20 CDT)
Evan objected to the coupling purchase on shipping economics — "i dont want
to pay $10 shipping for a $0.75 part" — then, after a failed hunt for a
cheaper commercial source, asked for a printed one: "make an STL file from
that spline to the female end of a lego axel." Built it, self-validated it,
and it is written to `cad/servo_lego_coupler_v1.stl`. **Nothing about its
strength is verified.**

## DG.1 The alternative-source hunt came back empty, which is itself the finding

Searched Amazon, eBay and AliExpress for a servo-spline-to-Lego-cross
adapter. Results: the Adafruit #4252 itself (via overseas resellers —
core-electronics.com.au, elmwoodelectronics.ca, smalldevices.com.au, all
worse for US shipping), the two printed designs the docs already reject
(Printables 61922/147626, Thingiverse equivalents), and nothing else. This
**confirms** what BOM row 22 already recorded rather than overturning it:
Adafruit is the sole commercial source. `docs/BOM.md:449`'s SparkFun
analysis had already noted the LEGO servo adapter as one of the four items
SparkFun does not stock; Adafruit has no free-shipping threshold, and
consolidating other items onto them makes their shipping worse, not better
(BOM's Adafruit section). So there is no bundling escape either.

An Adafruit forum thread titled "MG90S servo spline size" would likely have
settled the #4252-fits-MG90S question directly. It is behind a bot-check.
**Not bypassed** — left for Evan to open:
`https://forums.adafruit.com/viewtopic.php?t=95879`.

## DG.2 The one hard number this needed

MG90S output shaft: **20-tooth spline, ~4.8–4.9 mm outer diameter**
(SkyStar/TinyTronics datasheet; servodatabase). Splined, not round — which
is what makes the printed version hard, and is the reason the design below
does what it does.

## DG.3 The design, and the two things it deliberately refuses to do

`scripts/gen_servo_lego_coupler.py` → `cad/servo_lego_coupler_v1.stl`.
Ø10 × 16 mm (16 mm matches the #4252, so it drops into the same space):

| end | feature | why |
|---|---|---|
| servo, z 0–8 | Ø4.65 mm plain round bore | 0.20 mm under the spline; the metal spline cuts its own seat |
| middle, z 8–10 | Ø2.2 mm axial hole | screwdriver access to the servo's OWN retaining screw — zero new parts, and the coupler cannot walk off the shaft |
| Lego, z 10–16 | 5.00 × 2.00 mm cross socket, 6 mm deep | receives a REAL Lego axle |

**It prints no cross-axle profile, which is the whole point.** Appendix BV
measured a printed male cross at SF 0.57–0.96 — thin cruciform fins shearing
along layer lines — and `steering.md` permits socket-style printed adapters
only. This obeys that rule rather than quietly relitigating it: the printed
part is a thick-walled socket (2.50 mm wall at the socket, 2.68 mm at the
bore) and the cross profile belongs to the real Lego axle.

**It does not model the 20-tooth spline.** 20 teeth on a Ø4.85 mm circle is
a ~0.76 mm tooth pitch, under what a 0.4 mm nozzle resolves. A modelled
spline would print as a blurred round hole while claiming a fidelity it does
not have, so the bore is honestly a press fit instead.

## DG.4 Validation actually performed

The generator carries the same self-check as `gen_tolerance_coupon.py`
(closed + consistently-wound mesh, signed volume vs analytic, refuses to
write on failure). Real output:

    ring points: 72 (64 fill + exact cross corners)
    triangles  : 1152
    manifold   : duplicate-directed-edges=0 unmatched-edges=0  -> PASS
    volume     : 1015.1211 mm^3 (expected 1015.1211, rel.err 1.05e-14)  -> PASS
    OVERALL    : PASS

**That self-check has a hole, so it was not trusted alone**: `build()` and
`expected_volume()` both call `ring_cross()`, so a wrong cross profile
cancels out and passes silently. Three independent checks were run against
the profile from outside the module:

    socket area   : mesh 16.000000 vs analytic 16.000000 mm^2  PASS
                    (analytic = 2*(span*arm) - arm^2, two overlapping
                     rectangles minus the double-counted centre square)
    axle clearance: min 0.1000 max 0.2693 mm radial over a real 4.80 axle
    cross corners : 12/12 present at exact angles  PASS

The corner check matters more than it looks: the ring is sampled by angle,
and if the 12 corner angles were not forced into the sample list the concave
notches would round over, tightening exactly the corners a real axle needs
to seat.

## DG.5 What is NOT known, stated because the temptation is to skip it

**No safety factor is claimed for this part and none can be computed.** The
bore-to-spline grip is friction plus spline bite and has never been loaded.
This is a printed STOPGAP to try before spending $10.75, not a proven
replacement for the #4252 — and the #4252 has no published torque rating
either (Appendix DF), so neither option has a real margin. What protects
this joint is the existing rule that the servo never reaches stall
(`SERVO_US_SPAN` limiting, task 8c). If it slips, the upgrade is a
transverse M2 grub screw into the bore, **not** the MG996R, which makes the
coupling problem ~5× worse (BOM row 7).

Four constants are unmeasured and parameterised at the top of the generator:
`AXLE_ARM` 1.80 (Lego cross-axle arm thickness — community value, and the
authoritative source consulted, cailliau.org, documents only the 4.80 mm
across-the-cross span, which IS confirmed), `SPLINE_DIA` 4.85 (datasheet
range), `SOCKET_CLEAR` 0.20 and `BORE_INTERF` 0.20 (both provisional). The
right source for `SOCKET_CLEAR` is the M1.3 tolerance coupon's axle row,
**which has still not been printed** — so this part inherits that gap.

## DG.6 State

**Nothing ordered, nothing printed.** The BOM is unchanged at $402.45 —
row 22 still buys the #4252, because a printed part with no torque margin
does not retire a purchased part with no torque margin until one of them
survives a test. `cad/README.md` documents the part, its four unmeasured
constants, and PETG rather than PLA (Appendix BV's failing numbers were
computed against PLA).

# Appendix DI - M1.3 tolerance coupon printed (Bambu P1S, ABS): pin row PASS at 4.80mm, axle row FAILS at every diameter, v2 sweep regenerated (2026-09-05 16:23 CDT)
M1.3's tolerance coupon (`cad/tolerance_coupon_v1.stl`, print-ready since
2026-07-23) was printed and tested for the first time. Real result: the pin
row closed cleanly, the axle row didn't — every commanded diameter tested
was too loose, which is the exact "sweep brackets nothing" contingency the
coupon's own README anticipated. Fixed with a v2 sweep, not a guess.

## DH.1 Setup, as reported (no caliper data taken)

Printer **Bambu P1S**, filament **Bambu ABS, Black** — replacing PLA+PETG
as the standing chassis material (Evan, 2026-09-03/2026-09-05). 0.4 mm
nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, 2 walls (README suggests 3 — untested whether
this matters for hole dimension, only flagged), 10% gyroid infill, 99%
X/Y shrinkage compensation (Bambu Studio's ABS-specific setting — confirmed
with Evan, not assumed). Exact print date/time not separately recorded.

**No calipers were used.** Every verdict below is Evan's fit-by-feel
against the coupon's own pass criteria (firm-thumb-press-and-holds for
pins; free-spin-no-slop for axles), not a measured offset. This is a real
gap against the coupon's own procedure ("also caliper each hole's actual
printed diameter") — recorded as a gap, not backfilled with invented
numbers.

## DH.2 Row identification, resolved after three rounds of back-and-forth

Evan initially described results by "top to bottom" position and hole
count, which didn't disambiguate cleanly against the generator's own
row-identification scheme (marker-hole count, orientation-independent).
Confirmed by asking him to describe marker-hole counts directly:

    row 1 (2 small holes)  = AXLE sweep (5.20-5.70 mm, 6 diameters)
    row 2 (1 small hole)   = PIN sweep (4.80-5.30 mm, 6 diameters)
    row 3 (5 holes, no markers) = PITCH row (uniform 5.10 mm x5)

The first thing Evan reported testing ("5 holes in a line... spin very
smooth even with the entire weight of the coupon") turned out to be the
PITCH row, not the axle sweep — he'd run a Lego axle through the pitch
row's uniform 5.10 mm holes rather than the actual 5.20-5.70 mm sweep.
Caught before it got recorded as an axle-fit result under the wrong
diameter; this is exactly the kind of mislabeling this coupon gates
against, one level up (the record almost inherited it).

## DH.3 Results

**Pin row — PASS.** "Only the smallest 3 are a good fit with the smallest
one being the best." Reading the sweep values (4.80/4.90/5.00/5.10/5.20/
5.30): 4.80, 4.90, 5.00 mm all seat with firm-press-and-hold; 4.80 is best.
**Chosen pin offset: 4.80 mm** — with the caveat that 4.80 is the bottom of
the tested range, not a bracketed optimum; a smaller value might fit
better still, untested.

**Axle row — FAIL, all six.** "All the ones in the first row spin smooth,
even the smallest ones seems a bit big." 5.20 mm, the smallest of the v1
sweep, already spins with noticeable slop. The sweep brackets nothing at
the tight end — the coupon's own contingency plan ("edit the ranges... and
re-run rather than guessing beyond the ends of the sweep") applies, and
was followed rather than skipped.

**Pitch row — not tested as designed.** The beam-across-holes-1-2-then-1-5
dimensional-scaling check was not run; Evan's axle-through-the-pitch-row
test (see DH.2) stands in as informal evidence the pitch row's 5.10 mm
holes are also on the loose side for an axle, consistent with the axle
row's finding, but answers a different question than the one this row is
for. Scale factor remains unknown.

## DH.4 v2: why 4.80 mm is a floor, not a guess

A ROUND bore for a ROTATING cross-profile Lego axle cannot go below the
axle's tip-to-tip diagonal without the corners binding on every rotation.
That diagonal is the same ~4.8 mm figure commonly cited for the pin hole
(`gen_servo_lego_coupler.py`'s `AXLE_ARM`/cross-socket sizing already
leans on this). So 4.80 mm is a physical lower bound, not an arbitrary
step below 5.20 — going meaningfully below it risks a bore the axle can't
even enter, wasting sweep positions on "doesn't fit" rather than "fits but
tight."

**v2 moves the axle sweep to 4.80-5.30 mm** — the same range already
proven to work for a PIN. This asks a real question rather than assuming
an answer: does the diameter that holds a pin also free an axle? They are
different Lego parts (solid round peg vs. cross-shaped rotating shaft), so
the two fits are not guaranteed to land at the same number even at
identical commanded bore diameter.

`scripts/gen_tolerance_coupon.py` changed: `PIN_LO`/`AXLE_LO` extracted as
named constants (previously two separate magic numbers, 4.8 and 5.2,
inline in the sweep loops); `AXLE_LO` moved 5.2 -> 4.8; default output
path moved to `cad/tolerance_coupon_v2.stl` so v1's file and its (now
historical) measured results are never overwritten. Real run:

    manifold   : duplicate-directed-edges=0 unmatched-edges=0  -> PASS
    volume     : 43677.842 mm^3 (expected 43677.842, rel.err 6.66e-16) -> PASS
    OVERALL    : PASS
    wrote      : cad\tolerance_coupon_v2.stl (902484 bytes)
    axle row   : 4.80, 4.90, 5.00, 5.10, 5.20, 5.30 mm (2 marker holes)

## DH.5 State

**v1 printed and partially tested (pin PASS, axle FAIL-too-loose, pitch
not run as designed). v2 generated, validated, NOT yet printed.** Neither
coupon has been calipered. M1.3 stays open until v2's axle row closes and
the pitch-row scale check actually runs. `cad/README.md` carries both
result tables (v1 filled in from Evan's reports, v2 blank pending the next
print) so the next session doesn't have to reconstruct this from chat.

# Appendix DL - Rack swapped 7-stud to 13-stud: max steer genuinely 58deg (was 32), R_min 297.5mm to 116.2mm; SERVO_US_SPAN unvalidated on new rack (2026-09-05 22:20 CDT)
Evan: "new steering angle 67 degrees" — then, after two rounds of
clarification, a real answer: he replaced the steering's 7-stud gear rack
with a 13-stud one, and the wheel's actual deviation from straight ahead is
now 58°, up from 32°. Confirmed genuine before touching anything, because
the numbers involved are the exact pair this project already has a
documented history of confusing.

## Why this took three messages to record

1. "67 degrees" — ambiguous whether raw protractor reading or deviation.
   Asked; both readings computed (23° or 67° deviation) so Evan could just
   pick.
2. "sorry protractor reading is 32 degrees" — a full correction, not an
   answer to the format question. Applying the established convention
   (`steering.md`: 90° = straight ahead, deviation = 90 − reading) to a
   32° reading gives a 58° deviation. Before recording that, one more check:
   **32 + 58 = 90 exactly** — the new raw reading (32) is numerically
   identical to the OLD deviation, and the new deviation (58) is numerically
   identical to what `steering.md` already documents as the historical WRONG
   reading for the old measurement. That is too clean a coincidence to
   accept silently, given this project already lost a 2.6x turn-radius
   error to exactly this reading-vs-deviation confusion once (Appendix BQ's
   own note). Asked directly: did the mechanism change, or is this the same
   rig re-described backwards?
3. **"i used a 13 stud long gear rack instead of the 7 length old one so
   yes it is genuinely 58 degrees."** Real mechanical change. The
   32-and-58-are-complementary coincidence is exactly that — a coincidence
   of this particular remeasurement, not a sign of the old error recurring.

## What changed, and what didn't

**Changed:** max steer deviation, 32° -> 58°, a 13-stud rack replacing the
old 7-stud one. Wheelbase is unaffected (185.95mm, Appendices DD/DE) — nothing
about the wheelbase measurement depends on rack length.

    R_min = wheelbase / tan(max steer)
    old:  185.95 / tan(32) = 185.95 x 1.600 = 297.5 mm
    new:  185.95 / tan(58) = 185.95 x 0.625 = 116.2 mm

116.2mm is comfortably inside the frozen 500-670mm corner-radius band —
favorable, and (as always) not a substitute for T2's empirical turning
test on the rolling chassis, which still gates every corner tile.

**NOT changed, and NOT assumed changed:** whether the pinion still sweeps
~180 degrees lock-to-lock. `steering.md`'s existing SERVO_US_SPAN table
(300/450/500us -> pinion angle -> road-wheel angle -> R) was built and
measured against the OLD 7-stud rack. The 7-stud rack may well have been
the actual mechanical travel limit before, not the pinion or the MG90S
itself — a 13-stud rack has more linear travel available, and there is no
measurement yet showing where the NEW hard stop actually is, or whether
the wheel-angle-per-pinion-degree relationship is still the same linear
ratio the old table assumed (0.3556 = 32/90). Extrapolating either from
the old numbers would be a guess dressed as a measurement.

## The safety-relevant consequence

`uno_control.ino`'s `SERVO_US_SPAN = 450` and its 10% margin exist
specifically to keep the servo from driving into a Lego hard stop, which
stalls the servo and — per Appendix BV's own numbers — puts the steering
coupler at SF 0.57-0.96, i.e. already marginal at the OLD rack's stall
torque. That margin was sized against hard-stop positions that may no
longer be correct. **This is now a real, safety-relevant open item, not
just a documentation gap**: PRD task 8c(i)'s calibration must be re-run on
the bench against the new rack before the servo is commanded anywhere near
its old span. Not attempted here — it needs Evan's hands and a protractor
on the actual new hardware, the same way the original 180-degree pinion
sweep and the original 32-degree wheel angle were each measured by him
directly.

## Corrected in place

`steering.md`: top-of-file warning banner rewritten (it previously named
32/58 as THE historical trap pair in the old sense — now that 58 is a
legitimate new deviation on different hardware, the banner needed to say
which rack a number belongs to, not just "trust 32, distrust 58"); the old
MAX STEER ANGLE bullet struck with a superseding note (not deleted — it was
correct for the hardware it described); the SERVO_US_SPAN table flagged as
7-stud-specific with an explicit warning against extrapolating a "58 row"
into it; the wheelbase section's R_min recomputed; a new dated section
added with the full derivation and the pinion-sweep caveat.
`docs/Project Record` mentions of 32 degrees from prior appendices are left
as written — they were true when written, describing the 7-stud rack.
`HANDOFF.md` (three places: max-steer constraint row, wheelbase row, the
T1-T6 track-fabrication row, the T2 naming-collision callout) and
`PRD_ROADMAP.md` (task 4's measured-geometry block, T2's estimate, the
M2.8-adjacent MG90S/pinion-sweep line, task 8c(i)'s new blocker) all
updated to match. `.claude/codebase-memory/track.md`'s corner-geometry
paragraph was also stale on car width and wheelbase independent of this
change; corrected in the same pass since it directly quotes the R_min
formula.

## State

**Nothing built, nothing ordered.** The steering rack swap is a real,
physical, already-completed change to hardware Evan is hand-assembling;
this project has no way to verify it independently. The two closed numbers
from this session (M1.3's pin/axle bore offsets) are unaffected — they are
about hole diameters, not steering geometry. Corner geometry remains
frozen pending T2. The pinion-sweep and SERVO_US_SPAN re-calibration on the
new rack is now the most safety-relevant open item in the steering
subsystem.

**Not recorded as fact and no firmware or geometry number changed on it**

# Appendix DN - Correction to DM: 58deg/270deg both measured with no servo attached -- real wheel-angle ceiling is ~38.7deg estimate, 45deg target may be unachievable (2026-09-05 22:57 CDT)
Correction to Appendix DM, same day. Asked Evan which physical shaft his
"~270 degrees" figure described: "the shaft that the servo will be
connected too." Confirms the pinion, as suspected — but a follow-up
question about HOW the 58 degree wheel figure (Appendix DL) was measured
surfaced something DM did not know to check: "no servo involved."

## DN.1 What this means

Both load-bearing numbers from today (58 deg wheel deviation, ~270 deg
pinion sweep) were hand-measured on the bare linkage with the servo
disconnected. They describe what the RACK's own physical ends allow, not
what the actual MG90S can drive. The MG90S is a fixed-spec 180 degree
servo (90 degrees each way) -- a property of the PART, unrelated to the
rack -- and that number does not grow just because the rack now allows
more travel.

The rack (135 degrees each way, from the new 270 degree figure divided by
two) now travels further than the servo can ever reach (90 degrees each
way). This is the mirror image of the old situation, where rack and servo
were both ~180 degrees and closely matched (Appendix BU: "an MG90S at 180
degrees is an EXACT 1:1 match to this rack -- no gearing, no reduction,
nothing").

## DN.2 The corrected estimate

Using the same linear pinion-to-wheel ratio this project has assumed
throughout (unverified, flagged every time it's used):

    ratio = 58 / 135 = 0.4296  (wheel degrees per pinion degree)
    servo-achievable wheel deviation ~= 90 x 0.4296 = 38.7 deg
    R_min at 38.7 deg = 185.95 / tan(38.7) = 232.4 mm

    for reference: reaching a TRUE 45 deg wheel angle would need
    45 / 0.4296 = 104.7 deg of pinion rotation -- the servo only has 90.

**Appendix DM's 45 degree planning target is not a safe margin below the
58 degree mechanical max -- it may not be achievable by this servo at
all.** The rack is no longer the binding constraint on this build (it has
slack the servo can't use); the servo's own 90-degree-each-way limit is.

## DN.3 What is and is not known

38.7 degrees is an ESTIMATE from an assumption (linearity between pinion
angle and wheel angle) that has never been verified and has real reason to
be doubted at large angles -- rack-and-pinion-to-tie-rod geometry is not
generally linear, the existing linear model was fit to three points on the
OLD, shorter rack, and this estimate extrapolates it onto a mechanism that
has since changed twice (Appendix DL, and now this). **The only way to get
a real number is to bench-measure the wheel angle with the actual MG90S
attached and driven to its own safe span** -- not computed from the
bare-linkage figures. This sharpens, rather than replaces, the
SERVO_US_SPAN re-calibration Appendix DL already flagged as the next real
task: measure the WHEEL angle directly, at the servo's real limits, once
mounted.

**What DM got right and this does not undo**: the rack's own hard stop is
further away than the servo can reach, so the risk of driving the coupler
into the rack's END is reduced by the longer rack, not worsened. The open
question was always how much wheel angle the servo itself yields -- that
number is now understood to be smaller than 58, not larger, and possibly
smaller than the 45 degree target Evan asked for.

## DN.4 Corrected in place

`steering.md`'s new dated section from Appendix DM (the 45 degree planning
cap) is struck with a pointer here rather than silently edited to a new
number -- the 45/185.95mm figures were a real, stated decision at the
time, now known to rest on an unachievable premise. Live docs
(HANDOFF.md, PRD_ROADMAP.md) updated to match. `docs/Project Record`
Appendix DM is left as written -- append-only, and it was an honest
record of the decision as understood at the time.

## DN.5 State

**Nothing built, nothing bench-tested.** The real wheel-angle ceiling with
the actual servo mounted is unmeasured. 38.7 degrees (R_min 232.4mm) is
the working estimate until Evan measures it directly; both remain
comfortably inside the frozen 500-670mm corner band regardless of exactly
where the true number lands, so this does not block anything today -- but
building to a 45 degree target the servo may not reach would be a real
mistake to carry into M1.5 CAD work.

# Appendix DO - Servo candidate found for the full 135deg range: HOOYIJ MG90D 270deg, same 20T spline as MG90S, not yet ordered (2026-09-05 23:11 CDT)
Evan asked directly for a servo covering the full 135°-each-way range the
new rack allows (Appendix DN found the MG90S caps out at 90° each way,
leaving an estimated ~38.7° at the wheel instead of the intended range).
Found a strong, well-specified candidate.

## Candidate: HOOYIJ MG90D, 270°, $16.99/4-pack ($4.25/unit)

Full spec sheet pulled from the live Amazon listing (B0D5YBL2JX), not a
summary snippet:

| spec | MG90D-270 | MG90S (current BOM row 7) | match? |
|---|---|---|---|
| horn gear spline | **20T, 4.9mm dia** | 20T, ~4.8-4.9mm (SkyStar/TinyTronics, Appendix DG) | SAME CLASS — existing coupler design (Adafruit #4252 and the printed `servo_lego_coupler_v1.stl`, both sized for a 4.85mm 20T spline) should fit without redesign |
| gear material | Full metal (aluminium) | Metal (the stated reason MG90S was chosen) | same |
| stall torque | 2.2 kg-cm @ 6V | ~2.2 kg-cm @ 4.8V (steering.md) | same class — does NOT worsen the coupler SF problem (Appendix BV) the way the MG996R fallback does |
| voltage | 4.8-6.0V | 4.8-6.0V (nominal) | same |
| weight | 13.5g | 13.4g | same |
| size | 22.4 x 12.1 x 22.8mm | ~22.8 x 12.2 x 31mm (varies by source) | third dimension differs — physically verify before assuming the existing mount fits unmodified |
| bearing | **None stated** | not documented either way in this project's notes | unverified both ways, not a new gap |
| price | $16.99/4 ($4.25 ea) | $7.99/2 ($4.00 ea) | comparable |

**The pulse-width-to-angle mapping is the actual point of this find**:
500-2500us = full 270°; 500-1500us OR 1500-2500us (either HALF of that
pulse range, split at the 1500us neutral) = 135°+/-3 deg. In this
project's firmware terms (`uno_control.ino`: `SERVO_US_CENTRE=1500`,
`SERVO_US_SPAN` = "+/- from centre"), the geometric max span for this part
would be **1000us**, driving the pinion through +/-135 deg -- matching the
new rack's measured travel (Appendix DN) with no wasted range on either
side, if centering is good.

## What this would fix, if adopted

Appendix DN's core problem was a mismatch: the rack now travels further
(135 deg each way) than the MG90S can reach (90 deg each way), capping
the real wheel angle at an unverified ~38.7 deg estimate instead of
something closer to the 58 deg the bare linkage allows. A 270 deg servo
at this spec removes that mismatch entirely -- the servo would no longer
be the binding constraint, the rack's own hard stop would be (same
favourable direction Appendix DM/DN already noted: hitting the servo's own
limit is safer than hitting a mechanical hard stop, and here the two
would land close together by design instead of the servo stopping short).

## What is NOT resolved by finding this part

- **Not ordered. Not bench-tested. Not confirmed to physically fit the
  existing mount** (`docs/WIRING_PROTOSHIELD.md`'s servo mount, sized
  against MG90S's footprint) -- the differing third dimension above needs
  a real caliper check against the mount, not an assumption.
- **One negative review flags 3-of-4 dead on arrival** from this listing
  (26 ratings, 4.2/5 average) -- a real quality-control risk at this price
  point. The 4-pack already buys built-in spares, which mitigates it
  somewhat without extra cost.
- **The bench measurement Appendix DL/DN called for is still needed
  regardless of which servo is used** -- wheel angle must be measured with
  the real servo attached and driven to its actual limit, not assumed from
  a datasheet pulse-width table.
- **This is a candidate, not a BOM change.** Per this project's standing
  rule (no hardware purchase without Evan's explicit go), `docs/BOM.md` row
  7 still names the MG90S. Flagged here and in `steering.md` as the
  recommended replacement pending Evan's confirmation.

## Two sibling listings noted, not deep-specced

Same brand's **TS90MD, 270°, $17.99/4-pack** and **RCmall's 180/270/360
configurable 9g servo, $19.58/5-pack** turned up in the same search --
both plausible alternates if the MG90D's DOA-rate review is a concern, not
individually verified to the same depth as the recommended candidate above.

## State

**Nothing ordered, nothing changed in the BOM.** `steering.md` updated
with the candidate and its fit against the coupler spline; `docs/BOM.md`
row 7 left as the MG90S with a pointer to this finding, not silently
swapped.

# Appendix DS - Track floor-fit self-check closed at its root cause: two definitions of usable width in one file (2026-09-06, ~13:43 CDT)
**The failing check was never about the car being too wide.** `cad/track_layout_v2.py`
held two different definitions of usable width in one file:

- `best_straight()` sized the straight run between corners against
  `FLOOR - 2*WALL_MARGIN` = **2800 mm**, the whole usable floor.
- `self_check()` demanded the span leave **100 mm** of that 2800 unused.

They had never agreed. The `MAX_STRAIGHT = 200 mm` cap bound first and hid the
disagreement while lane was 229.5 mm (171 mm spare). When the 13-stud rack
rebuild pushed the front track to 155 mm and lane to 310 mm (Appendix DM), the
80.5 mm of slack that was masking it was consumed exactly. Span 2710 mm, spare
90 mm, required 100 mm, `AssertionError` at line 315.

## The fix

1. **New constant `SPARE_MIN = 0.100`**, and `best_straight()` now RESERVES it.
   This is the structural half: the layout self-corrects from here — a future
   width increase shrinks the straight instead of failing the check, and it only
   fails when the straight hits 0 and the span still does not fit, which is a
   genuine geometric failure worth failing on.
2. **`MAX_STRAIGHT` 200 -> 190 mm.** Needed for two reasons, not one. At 200,
   `best_straight` returns exactly 195 mm and the span lands on exactly 2.700 m,
   while the assert's right-hand side (`3.000 - 0.200 - 0.100`) evaluates to
   `2.6999999999999997` in float — **it fails on the boundary.** 190 also leaves
   110 mm of real spare rather than sitting on the 100 mm floor.
3. **Line 315 now uses the constant** plus the `1e-9` epsilon that lines
   295/303/347 already carry.

## Real output, not projected

    track_layout_v2 self_check: PASS
    floor           3.000 x 3.000 m (usable 2.800)
    car width       155.00 mm  FRONT track, MEASURED 2026-09-05 (Appendix DM) ...
    lane width      310 mm
    street pitch    1190 mm  (straight between corners 190 mm)
    span            2690 mm of 2800 usable -> 110 mm SPARE
    driven route    figure-8 through the centre intersection, 8.23 m

Across the frozen 500-670 mm band, from the patched module:

| R (mm) | straight | pitch | span | spare | spare >= 100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **500** | **190** | **1190** | **2690** | **110** | **yes** |
| 550 | 95 | 1195 | 2700 | 100 | yes |
| 600 | 0 | 1200 | 2710 | 90 | **no** |
| 670 | 0 | 1340 | 2990 | -190 | REFUSES (SystemExit) |

## Two things this session found that were not in HANDOFF

**1. The derived artifacts had been silently frozen since 2026-09-05.** `main()`
calls `self_check()` BEFORE it writes, so the failing assert meant
`cad/track_layout_v2.svg` and `.json` never regenerated. The committed JSON still
read `car_width 0.14825 / lane 0.2965 / span 2.6965` — one revision behind the
155 mm car. Both regenerated now. The print plan grew with the lane:
intersection boxes 10.67 -> 11.16 m, tiles 85 -> 88, filament ~1051 -> ~1081 g,
route 8.31 -> 8.23 m. (Self-check 8's `filament_g < 2000` still passes.)

**2. `cad/vehicle_envelope.py` duplicated four of the constants** (`FLOOR`,
`WALL_MARGIN`, `STREETS`, `MAX_STRAIGHT`) while its own `max_car_width`
docstring says the two scripts "have to agree." Changing `MAX_STRAIGHT` in one
file alone would have left it printing "200 mm is the cap track_layout_v2.py
uses" — false, and silently so. Mirrored the constant AND added a guard to its
`self_check()` that lazily imports `track_layout_v2` (inside the function, so a
normal run stays stdlib-only and does not pull numpy) and asserts the four
constants match.

**The guard was proven to fire, not assumed to.** Monkeypatching the drift back
in:

    GUARD FIRES: MAX_STRAIGHT has drifted: track_layout_v2.py says 0.19,
    this file says 0.2. One track, two scripts - they must agree.

## What is NOT closed

⚠️ **At R=600 the straight is already 0 mm and spare is 90 mm — under
`SPARE_MIN`, with nothing left to shrink.** The fix does not hide this and does
not solve it. A T2 turning test returning a radius near 600 mm reopens the
floor-fit as a real problem, and the self-check asserts only the R=500 case, so
it will not catch that on its own. Corner geometry stays FROZEN until T2
regardless.

## Stale doc text corrected as a consequence of the change

- The header docstring's span table (`R=500 -> span 2780 mm FITS`, `550 -> 2980
  NO`, `600 -> 3180 NO`) came from the over-constrained `2R + lane` pitch that
  **Appendix AY already corrected** — self-check 2 has tested 500/550/600 all
  building ever since, and the docstring never caught up. It contradicted the
  code below it before this session; rewritten with real output rather than left
  contradicting the numbers this entry adds.
- `main()` printed `car width 155.00 mm MEASURED 2026-09-03 (rear track; body
  135.75 and front 107.5 are both narrower)` — self-contradicting output (it
  printed 155 while calling it rear track and front 107.5). Corrected to name
  the front track and Appendix DM.

## 3DStreet: blocked this session, and the failure mode is diagnostic

Evan asked for 3DStreet work after this fix. **Zero `mcp__3dstreet__*` tools
exist in this session** — three separate `ToolSearch` queries returned nothing.
`.mcp.json` does configure the server (`npx -y 3dstreet-mcp`). The relay's own

# Appendix DT - 3DStreet pairing mid-session proven insufficient; marking table recomputed and the model scale turns out to be derived, not chosen (1:11.80) (2026-09-06, ~13:57 CDT)
Evan asked to start making street layouts, and paired the 3DStreet tab
mid-session. Two results: the 3DStreet blocker is now diagnosed rather than
suspected, and the marking table PRD_ROADMAP itself flags as stale is
recomputed and runnable.

## 1. 3DStreet: mid-session pairing is NOT sufficient. Appendix DQ confirmed a second time.

Evan paired the tab. The 3DStreet page's own status feed reported
**"MCP relay paired"** and logged **four `tools/list: Completed`** calls — the
relay answered every one. The `3dstreet` MCP server also reconnected mid-session
and its server instructions reappeared in context.

**And the session still has ZERO `mcp__3dstreet__*` tools.** Six `ToolSearch`
queries across this session, two of them after the pairing and after the
reconnect.

That is a much stronger result than the previous "tools absent, tab maybe not
paired" reading. The relay is demonstrably answering `tools/list`, so the tool
definitions exist on the wire and **the session's own tool registry is what is
not picking them up.** Appendix DQ's diagnosis — a session's MCP registry is
fixed at startup — is confirmed from a second, independent direction, and
sharpened: **even a server disconnect/reconnect inside the session does not
re-register the tools.**

**Actionable rule, replacing "pair the tab and retry":** the 3DStreet tab must
be open and paired BEFORE the Claude session starts. Pairing afterwards cannot
be recovered from inside the session.

**One distractor worth naming so it does not cost a third session.** The page's
status bar reads **"WebMCP active (26 tools)"**. WebMCP is the page's PRIMARY
transport, which registers its tools with an *agentic browser* (ChatGPT's
desktop browser, Gemini in Chrome, Chrome 149+ behind
`chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing`). **That is not Claude Code.** Claude
Code uses the MCP relay, which the page itself labels "fallback for clients
without WebMCP". Reading "26 tools" as "Claude Code has 26 tools" is the
obvious wrong inference and it is right there on screen.

## 2. The marking table, recomputed — and the SCALE turns out to be derived, not chosen

`PRD_ROADMAP.md` says in its own words that "the marking table below is stale
and NOT yet recomputed". It was scaled **1:14 from an ESTIMATED 130 mm car**
(Appendix L, 2026-08-05). Since then the car has been measured four times, the
governing width flipped from rear track to front track (Appendix DM), and the
lane rule itself changed from a fixed scale to `lane = 2.0 x car width`
(`SIM_TRANSFER_SPEC` section 3).

**THE DIRECTION OF THE DERIVATION SILENTLY REVERSED, and nobody noticed.**

- Appendix L picked the SCALE first (1:14) and derived the lane from it:
  12 ft / 14 = 261.3 mm.
- The lane rule that replaced it derives the LANE from the car (2.0 x 155 mm =
  310 mm), which means the scale is no longer free — it is whatever makes the
  model lane represent a real lane.

**Why the swap went unnoticed for a month:** at the 130 mm car of the era the
two rules agree almost exactly — the lane rule gives 260.0 mm and a scale of
1:14.07 against the published 261 mm at 1:14. They only diverge as the car
grows. At today's 155 mm car:

    scale = 12 ft / 310 mm = 1:11.80

**1:14 is not a decision that was revisited and kept. It is one that was
overtaken.** Nothing physical has been cut or printed to it, so correcting it
now costs nothing. It also independently confirms Appendix AM's offhand
estimate that this track runs at "roughly 1/11".

### New file: `cad/marking_specs.py` (parametric, self-checking, stdlib-only)

Real output at the measured 155 mm car:

| feature | full scale (MUTCD) | model @ 1:11.80 |
|---|---|---|
| lane width | 12 ft | **310.0 mm** (the input, not an output) |
| normal line | 4-6 in | **8.61 - 12.92 mm** |
| stop line | 12-24 in | **25.83 - 51.67 mm** |
| dash, TRUE scale | 10 + 30 ft | 258 + 775 mm — **only 8.0 cycles per lap, REJECTED** |
| dash, USED | ratio only | **68.6 + 137.2 mm**, 40 cycles per lap |

Yellow separates opposing directions, white separates same-direction (MUTCD,
verified 2026-08-05, not recalled).

Seven groups of self-checks, `marking_specs self_check: PASS`. The two worth
naming:

- **A regression against Appendix L's six published 1:14 numbers**, which
  Appendix O.4's cold audit already re-verified ("all six MUTCD 1:14 numbers
  reproduce exactly"). It pins the scaling arithmetic independently of the
  scale. **This check found the direction-reversal above** — the first cut drove
  it from a 130 mm car width and failed at `14.067692307692308`, which is
  exactly the artefact of computing the scale from the lane rule instead of
  reading it off. Rewritten to drive from an explicit 1:14, which is what
  Appendix L actually did.
- **The same cross-file drift guard added to `vehicle_envelope.py` in Appendix
  DS**, now a third user: it lazily imports `track_layout_v2.py` inside the
  check (so a normal run stays stdlib-only) and asserts `CAR_WIDTH` and the lane
  agree. Proven to fire, not assumed:

      GUARD FIRES: CAR_WIDTH has drifted: track_layout_v2.py says 0.155,
      this file says 0.148. One track, two scripts - they must agree.

### THE DASH RATIO IS UNRESOLVED, AND THE RECORD CONTRADICTS ITSELF

This blocks printing any dashed marking, and it is a documentation defect, not
an open design question.

- `HANDOFF.md`, `track.md` and Appendix L all record the deviation as
  **"Duckietown uses ~2:1"** — and **not one of them says which side is which.**
- MUTCD's ratio is **dash:gap = 1:3** (10 ft dash, 30 ft gap). "2:1" could mean
  gap:dash = 2:1 (dash 1 : gap 2, denser than MUTCD, plausible) or dash:gap =
  2:1 (dash LONGER than its gap, which no road marking does).
- **Appendix L's own worked example — "~60 mm dash / 180 mm gap" — is 1:3.**
  It kept MUTCD's ratio and never applied the 2:1 at all. So the appendix that
  introduced the 2:1 deviation contradicts it two paragraphs later.

`marking_specs.py` defaults to `DASH_TO_GAP = 0.5` (gap twice the dash) as the
reading that is both a plausible parse of "2:1" and denser than MUTCD, which was
the entire point of the deviation. **It is flagged in-code and in the printed
output as a DEFAULT, not a decision.** `--dash-to-gap` changes it and the table
follows. A self-check asserts the dash is never longer than its gap.

`TARGET_DASH_CYCLES = 40` (dash cycles the car should see in one 8.23 m lap) is
an EST and is the other free parameter — it, not the ratio, sets the absolute
size.

## 3. Correction to what I told Evan earlier in this session

I said the effective scale was **"~1:10"**, derived by assuming a 3.1 m real
lane. **Using MUTCD's actual 12 ft standard — which is what Appendix L used and
what this project's marking table has always been built on — it is 1:11.80.**
The 1:10 figure came from picking a round real-lane width rather than the
standard one. 1:11.80 is the number; it is also much closer to the old 1:14 than
1:10 was, so the correction is smaller than I implied.

# Appendix DU - Dash ratio DECIDED: dash:gap = 1:2, closing an ambiguity that sat in three documents for a month (2026-09-06, ~14:02 CDT)
**Evan: "1:2".** Closes the ambiguity Appendix DT flagged one entry earlier,
and it was the last thing blocking any dashed marking from being printed.

**dash:gap = 1:2** — the gap is twice the dash. At the derived 1:11.80 scale on
the 8.23 m lap that is **68.6 mm dash / 137.2 mm gap**, 40 cycles per lap.

**What the decision actually resolves.** The project had recorded the deviation
as "Duckietown uses ~2:1" in three separate places — Appendix L, `HANDOFF.md`,
and `track.md` — and **not one of them said which side was which.** MUTCD's is
dash:gap = 1:3 (10 ft dash, 30 ft gap). "2:1" admitted two readings:

- gap:dash = 2:1, i.e. dash:gap = 1:2 — denser than MUTCD. **This is the call.**
- dash:gap = 2:1 — a dash longer than its own gap, which no road marking uses.

Worse, **Appendix L's own worked example (60 mm dash / 180 mm gap) is 1:3** — it
kept MUTCD's ratio and never applied the 2:1 it had just introduced. The
appendix contradicted itself, and that contradiction propagated into two live
documents and survived a month.

Evan's reading is the one that makes the deviation do its job: MUTCD's 1:3 was
rejected because at this scale it gives too few dashes for a CNN seeing 64x64,
so the replacement has to be DENSER, not sparser. 1:2 is denser; 2:1 would have
been a different thing entirely.

**Not claimed as MUTCD compliance.** It is a documented deliberate deviation,
exactly as Appendix L intended — the difference is that it is now a single
unambiguous number instead of a phrase that parsed two ways.

`cad/marking_specs.py` carries it as a decision rather than a default now
(docstring, the `DASH_TO_GAP` constant, and the printed output all say so).
`--dash-to-gap` still re-runs the table at any other ratio. `self_check: PASS`,
including the assert that a dash may never be longer than its gap.

# Appendix DV - 3DStreet startup rule confirmed by restart; the track has ONE lane, so DU's dash decision had nothing to mark; dashed edge lines chosen (2026-09-06, ~15:58 CDT)
First 3DStreet work that actually touched the scene, after a restart with the
tab already paired. Three findings, one of them a defect in a decision made
40 minutes earlier in this same session.

## 1. The startup rule is CONFIRMED — restart with the tab paired works

Appendix DT predicted it; this session tested it deliberately rather than by
luck. Evan restarted Claude with the 3dstreet.app tab already open and paired.
**All 26 `mcp__3dstreet__*` tools registered on the first `ToolSearch`.**

That closes the loop opened 2026-09-01 and chased across four sessions:

| condition | tools registered? |
|---|---|
| server unapproved | no (Appendix BB) |
| server approved, tab paired, session started BEFORE pairing | **no** (DQ's original miss, and DT) |
| server approved, tab paired mid-session, server even reconnected | **no** (DT — six ToolSearch queries) |
| **server approved, tab paired, session started AFTER** | **YES** (DQ 2026-09-06, and reproduced here) |

**The rule is now tested in both directions, not just observed once.**

## 2. THE TRACK HAS ONE LANE, AND APPENDIX DU'S DASH DECISION HAD NOTHING TO MARK

This is a defect in DU, written earlier today. I asked Evan to decide the dash
ratio without first establishing how many lanes the track has.

The chain, all from existing project sources:

- `docs/SIM_TRANSFER_SPEC.md` section 3 sets **lane : vehicle = 2.0x**, and
  benchmarks it against "US highway lane (12 ft = 3658 mm) / typical car body
  (~1850 mm) = 1.98x". So **310 mm is ONE lane**, not a road.
- `cad/track_layout_v2.py` uses `lane` exactly once, in
  `span = (streets - 1) * pitch + lane`, i.e. as the road's TOTAL width. The
  generator models a **single-lane road**.
- A single-lane road has no centreline. Appendix L's "yellow separates opposing
  directions" therefore applies to **nothing on this track**, and MUTCD edge
  lines are SOLID, so a dashed line had no home either.
- Two lanes would be 620 mm. Span goes 2690 -> 3000 mm against 2800 mm usable:
  **the 3x3 grid would not fit at all.** Two lanes is not available without
  changing the floor or the grid.

So DU's `dash:gap = 1:2` was correct arithmetic attached to a marking the track
did not have. Caught by building the cross-section in 3DStreet, which is exactly
the use HANDOFF reserved it for.

**RESOLVED by Evan the same session: option 2 — single lane, DASHED edge lines.**
The alternatives were (1) solid edges and no dash anywhere, which throws away
the longitudinal signal the compression exists to provide, and (3) two lanes,
which does not fit the floor. **This is a SECOND deliberate deviation stacked on
the first**: the ratio compression (DU) deviates from MUTCD's 1:3, and now the
placement deviates too — MUTCD edge lines are solid, and a dashed edge line in
the real standard means something specific (a lane ending, or a passing-zone
boundary). Neither deviation is claimed as compliance.

## 3. 3DStreet's striping enum accepts invalid values SILENTLY

Worth its own note because the read-back does not catch it.

`striping: "dashed"` was accepted by `managedStreetUpdate`, and
`getManagedStreet` echoed it back verbatim — so the read-back looked like
confirmation. **It rendered as a solid line.** Only a close-up snapshot showed
the failure; the plan view at 53.3 m ground extent could not resolve dashes
either way, and an intermediate check wrongly read as "probably fine".

The real ids come from `listMixins` category **`lane-separator`**:
`solid-stripe`, `dashed-stripe`, `short-dashed-stripe`,
`short-dashed-stripe-yellow`, `solid-doubleyellow`, `solid-dashed`,
`solid-dashed-yellow`, `crosswalk-zebra`.

**`short-dashed-stripe` renders correctly** — verified by close-up, dashes
clearly visible on both edges.

**Operational rule: a `getManagedStreet` read-back proves a value MOUNTED, not
that it is VALID.** Verify striping and stencil ids visually, at close-up
range, or check them against `listMixins` first.
