# Appendix EK - LaneMaker boundary, one more timeboxed try: the straight-through connector trim is exactly length/24 (5/5 samples, machine precision) but it covers only 1 of ~4 unresolved pieces -- not implemented (2026-09-07 ~11:17 CDT)
**WHAT:** One more timeboxed attempt at the LaneMaker `<junction><boundary>` trim
(Appendix EH's open item), per the "only evidence has ever been right" method
rule. Found a genuine, precise sub-pattern in `~/Downloads/1122.xodr`
(Evan's own LaneMaker export, ground truth) that was not in the record before
-- but it does not add up to a working fix, and nothing was implemented in
`cad/export_xodr.py`.

**METHOD:** Parsed every `<road length=...>` and every `<boundary><segment
.../>` in the reference file (5 junctions, 15 "lane"-type boundary segments
across junctions 0-4), and computed `start_trim = sStart` and
`end_trim = length - sEnd` for each.

**THE FINDING:** Five of the fifteen segments (roads 4, 2, 20, 25, 49) --
each independently confirmed to be a **straight-through connecting road**
(`<line/>` geometry linking one street directly to another, not a turn arc)
-- have `start_trim == end_trim == road_length / 24`, matching to 10-12
significant figures:

| road | length (m) | trim (m) | trim / length |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4  | 22.762907957366529 | 0.94845449822360617 | 0.041666... |
| 2  | 22.762907957366529 | 0.94845449822360628 | 0.041666... |
| 20 | 22.749895796034284 | 0.94791232483476551 | 0.041666... |
| 25 | 22.819218983688788 | 0.9508007909870374  | 0.041666... |
| 49 | 22.749953519664004 | 0.94791472998600013 | 0.041666... |

`length/24` beats the competing hypothesis "trim is just a fixed ~0.949 m
constant" -- the constant-hypothesis only matches these five to ~3
significant figures (spread 0.9479-0.9508), `length/24` matches to
10-12. This is the first trim relationship this project has found that
holds to machine precision rather than "close enough to eyeball."

**WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, so nothing was built on it:**
1. **It only covers ONE of at least two trim families.** The other 10
   boundary segments (roads 21, 16, 9, 24, 43, 34, 36, 31, 53, 48 -- all
   turn-arc connectors, not straight-through) cluster around 1.0-1.55 m of
   absolute trim with no clean formula found in this timebox; they do NOT
   fit `length/24` (that would predict 0.44-0.55 m, roughly half the actual
   values).
2. **The reference file's junctions 0/1/2/4 are 2-3-arm topologies**, not
   the plain 4-way crossings our own grid needs at its 1 interior junction
   (8 of our 9 junctions are corner/edge junctions with 2-3 arms and NO
   opposite-arm partner, so no straight-through connector exists for most
   of their arms at all -- `length/24` would apply to 0 of those arms).
   Junction 3's structure (four arms, one incoming road with FOUR
   connecting roads) was not decoded either.
3. **Generalizability is unconfirmed.** All 5 samples come from one export,
   at one lane width. Whether `1/24` is a LaneMaker constant or an artifact
   of this specific file's lane-width/geometry has no second data point to
   test -- would need a second reference export at a different lane width.
4. Selection rule (WHICH connecting road represents an arm when several
   exist) and the `side` attribute logic remain undecoded, same as EG/EH.

**VERDICT:** Real, verified new evidence -- not the 5th guess. But it closes
at most 1 of the ~4 unresolved pieces needed for a working boundary block,
and covers a minority of our own junctions' arms even where it does apply.
Implementing a boundary generator now would still mean guessing on the
majority of arms, repeating the exact "hypothesis wrong" pattern Appendix EH
already flagged. **Not implemented. Standing recommendation to bank the
exporter as "loads and renders; simulation unsupported" still holds.**

**If pursued further, the next real step is external to this session:**
export a SECOND reference file from LaneMaker's GUI with a different lane
width (or built by hand around a simple 4-arm crossing) to test whether
`length/24` survives a scale change, and to get a clean 4-way sample for the
turn-arc family. That is Evan's own LaneMaker session, not something
derivable from the one file on disk.

# Appendix EL - LaneMaker boundary, tried again: side does not follow any simple positional pattern across 5 junctions -- still not enough to build even one junction without guessing (2026-09-07 ~11:43 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan asked to try the LaneMaker boundary again, a second time in the
same session (after Appendix EK). Checked whether EK's `length/24` trim
finding was enough, on its own, to build a boundary for at least one
COMPLETE junction in our own grid without guessing. It is not — `side` is
also load-bearing and does not follow any of the simple patterns tested.
**Nothing implemented in `cad/export_xodr.py`; no file regenerated.**

**Which junction was the target.** Our `--junctions` grid has 1 four-way
(interior) + 4 three-way (edge) + 4 two-way (corner) junctions
(`cad/export_xodr.py::junction_layout`). Only the four-way junction has a
straight-through connector (`r_arc is None`, `elif abs(cross) < 1e-9` branch)
for EVERY arm — the 3-way and 2-way junctions have at least one arm with no
opposite partner, so most of their boundary segments would need the turn-arc
family EK already found has no discovered formula. The four-way junction was
therefore the one candidate for a fully evidence-backed (not guessed) boundary
block.

**`side` tested against `1122.xodr`'s 5 junctions, position by position:**

| junction | joint sequence (L=left, R=right) |
|---|---|
| 0 (2 arms) | **L**, R |
| 1 (3 arms) | **L**, R, R |
| 2 (3 arms) | R, **L**, R |
| 3 (4 arms) | **L**, **L**, R, R |
| 4 (3 arms) | **L**, R, **L** |

No positional rule survives all five: not "first is always left" (junction 2
breaks it), not "one left per junction" (junction 3 has two), not "left
count scales with arm count" (junction 4 has 3 arms and 2 lefts, junction 1
has 3 arms and 1 left). `side` almost certainly encodes which side of the
connecting road's own reference line the joint point falls on — a real
geometric fact from LaneMaker's internal boundary-polygon computation — but
that requires reproducing the polygon computation itself, not a lookup table
from 5 samples.

**VERDICT: still not evidence, so still not built.** EK already flagged
`side` as unresolved; this attempt turned that into a tested, ruled-out set
of simple hypotheses rather than an open question, but the trim finding does
not carry the whole boundary on its own. Implementing even the one
"fully-evidenced" junction would mean guessing `side` on all four of its
joints — the exact repeat of the "4 hypotheses, 4 wrong" pattern Appendix EH
already named.

**The one path that isn't guessing:** build ONE plain 4-way crossing by hand
in LaneMaker's own GUI (not a SampleMap, not our exporter) and read the
`side` values it writes. That is a ground-truth read, the same method that
already resolved the one-way-connecting-road requirement (Appendix EF) and
the `roadRunnerProfile` schema. It needs Evan's own LaneMaker session — nothing
here can substitute for it.

**Standing recommendation unchanged:** bank the exporter as "loads and
renders; simulation unsupported." Next real move on this thread is the
hand-built-junction export above, not another read of the existing file.

# Appendix EM - Recreated 1122.xodr 1:1 at our scale: new rescale_reference_xodr.py scales every dimensioned attribute by one factor, leaves junction/boundary/side structure byte-identical -- untested in LaneMaker (2026-09-07 ~11:55 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan's instruction after EK/EL: stop deriving the boundary/`side`
semantics, `1122.xodr` "works perfectly, try to recreate it 1:1." Clarified
with Evan which "1:1" was meant (three options offered); chose: **rescale
the reference file itself, keep its exact topology, change nothing
structural.**

**NEW SCRIPT: `cad/rescale_reference_xodr.py`.** Parses `1122.xodr` and
multiplies every DIMENSIONED numeric attribute by one scale factor `k`,
leaving every structural element (junctions, connections, laneLink,
boundary segments, `side`, `type`, element order) byte-identical. This is a
documented, mechanical transform (OpenDRIVE's own geometry schema), not a
guess:

- `<geometry s x y length>`: all four `*= k`; `hdg` (an angle) untouched.
- `<arc curvature>`, `<spiral curvStart/curvEnd>`: `/= k` (radius `*= k`).
- `<paramPoly3>` (`pRange="normalized"`, confirmed the ONLY range used in
  this file, asserted in code): all 8 coefficients `*= k` uniformly, since
  the parameter `p` is dimensionless in [0,1].
- `<elevation>`, `<laneOffset>`, `<width>` (cubic-in-s polynomials whose
  output has dimension length): `s *= k`; `a *= k`; `b` unchanged;
  `c /= k`; `d /= k^2` (standard polynomial-rescaling algebra).
- `<roadMark sOffset width>`: both `*= k`.
- `<road length>`, `<segment sStart/sEnd>` (boundary): `*= k`.
- `roadRunnerProfile <section type_s>`: `*= k`, **except** the literal
  `4294967295` sentinel (UINT32_MAX terminator, Appendix EA), passed through
  unchanged — it is never a distance.
- `offsetX2` and every id/type/enum/contactPoint: untouched (a ratio and
  non-length fields are invariant under uniform scale).

**Bounding box, without curve evaluation.** Every geometry's start point
`(x,y)` plus a pad of its own `length` in each direction gives a safe outer
bbox (no arc/spiral/paramPoly3 can extend farther from its start than its
own arc length). Reference footprint (max of width/height): **129.334 m**.

**Run at `--target 2.7`** (our project's model-scale convention):
`k = 0.020876`. Output `cad/track_1122_rescaled.xodr`:

| | reference | rescaled |
|---|---|---|
| roads | 55 | 55 (unchanged) |
| junctions | 5 | 5 (unchanged) |
| boundary blocks | 5 | 5 (unchanged, side/type/order untouched) |
| footprint (est.) | 129.334 m | 2.700 m |
| total road length | 1055.139 m | 22.027 m |

**Verified, not asserted:**
- `self_check()`: scaling at k=0.1 moves the estimated footprint by exactly
  k (129.334 -> 12.933 m), confirming the transform is linear as designed.
- Element-tag counts identical between reference and output (`diff` on
  sorted/uniqued tag lists: empty).
- `hdg` values identical char-for-char (angles correctly left untouched).
- `offsetX2` values identical char-for-char.
- Lane width spot check: `a="3.25"` -> `a="0.06784754443936913"`,
  matches `3.25 * 0.020876` to full float precision.
- The `4294967295` sentinel count matches (8 in both files) and its value
  is unchanged where present.
- Output parses as well-formed XML (`ET.parse` succeeds).

**WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM:** this is Evan's own test map (5 junctions, an
arbitrary layout), resized -- not our project's 3x3 figure-8 track. If it
loads and simulates in LaneMaker, that confirms the rescale transform itself
introduces no new fault and unblocks testing the REST of the pipeline
(sim-transfer, etc.) on a real closed network; it does NOT answer EK/EL's
boundary-derivation question, and does not produce a track matching our
car's actual intended geometry. **Cannot be verified from this session** --
LaneMaker is a Windows GUI app with no automation tool available here; every
load/crash verdict in this project has come from Evan running it directly.

**File to test:** `D:\ClaudeCode\Autonomous Car Project\cad\track_1122_rescaled.xodr`

# Appendix EN - THE CRASH DID NOT HAPPEN: a boundary-carrying file reached spawn logic, so the boundary really was the cause; LaneMaker refuses short roads, which threatens our 1.46 m street segments; and my rescaler was silently skipping every road object (2026-09-07 ~12:06 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan tested the rescaled copies from Appendix EM in LaneMaker. Three
results, one of them the most important thing this thread has produced.

## 1. THE CRASH DID NOT HAPPEN. This is the headline.

`cad/track_1122_rescaled.xodr` (k=0.020876) **loaded, and simulation did not
crash.** No `0xC0000409 FAST_FAIL p=7`. It failed instead on a benign,
readable warning:

    [2026-09-07 11:57:35.328] [warning] No roads to spawn on!
    Try creating longer roads.

Four appendices (EE-EH) chased that crash on OUR generated grid, and EG/EH
left `<junction><boundary>` as "the last VISIBLE structural difference, which
does not make it the cause." **A file carrying a complete, valid boundary got
all the way to spawn logic.** That is the strongest evidence so far that the
boundary really was the cause -- but note precisely what it is worth: the
boundary in this file was COPIED, not derived, so this confirms the diagnosis
without supplying the fix. EK/EL's derivation problem is untouched.

## 2. SPAWN THRESHOLD: LaneMaker refuses roads that are too short

| k | shortest road | result |
|---|---|---|
| 0.020876 | 0.213 m | no spawn ("try creating longer roads") |
| 0.5 | **5.105 m** | **spawns** |

Threshold is somewhere in 0.213-5.105 m; not narrowed further because Evan
moved on. Reference untouched (k=1) has a 10.210 m shortest road.

⚠️ **DIRECT CONSEQUENCE FOR OUR OWN TRACK, and it is not a small one.** Our
grid's street segments are `pitch - 2*Rt` = 1100 - 2x500 = **100 mm at model
scale = 1.463 m at full scale** (x14.6304). That is FAR below the reference's
10.210 m and plausibly below LaneMaker's spawn threshold. **A car may be
unspawnable on our geometry no matter what the boundary block says** -- a
blocker nobody had identified, because every prior attempt crashed before
reaching spawn logic. If confirmed, the fix is geometric (raise pitch
relative to the 500 mm kerb return radius to lengthen street segments), not
structural.

## 3. A REAL DEFECT IN `rescale_reference_xodr.py`, found by Evan's eyes

Evan: the directional turn arrows rendered "off to the side instead of on the
road." **The script scaled no `<object>` element at all** -- the reference
carries 31 of them (`type="roadMark"`, `subtype="arrow"` and
`subtype="stopping-line"`). An arrow is
`<object s="10" t="3.25" width="2" .../>`, where `t` is lateral offset from
the reference line and 3.25 is exactly one lane width. At k=0.5 the lane
halved to 1.625 m while `t` stayed 3.25 m, putting every arrow **exactly 2x
too far out** -- the reported symptom, mechanism confirmed rather than
guessed. `s="10"` also landed past the end of a road now 5.105 m long, and a
2 m glyph sat on a 1.625 m lane.

A full element/attribute census of the reference found a SECOND miss:
`<laneSection s>`. Both fixed: `<object>` now scales
`s, t, zOffset, length, width, height, radius, validLength` and leaves
`hdg/pitch/roll/orientation` (angles) alone; `<laneSection s>` scales.

**The guard that would have caught it, added and PROVEN TO FIRE.**
`ATTR_CLASS` classifies every (tag, attribute) pair in the format as
length / inverse / poly / angle / opaque, and `check_coverage()` REFUSES to
scale a file containing an unclassified pair -- because the failure mode here
is silence, not an error. `self_check()` additionally verifies that **every
one of the 1202 length-class values in the file moved by exactly k**, which
is the assertion that fails if a future element is added to the format and
left out of `rescale()`. Verified firing on a synthetic
`<road superelevation="0.02">`.

Post-fix invariant, checked at three scales: arrow `t / lane_width = 1.000`
at k=1.0, 0.5 and 0.25 (it was 2.000 at k=0.5 before the fix).

## Files

- `cad/probe_spawn_k100.xodr` (k=1.0, shortest road 10.210 m, lane 3.250 m)
  -- a round-trip control: if this behaves exactly like the untouched
  reference, the transform is proven neutral.
- `cad/probe_spawn_k050.xodr` (k=0.5, 5.105 m, lane 1.625 m) -- the scale
  already known to spawn, now with arrows correct.
- `cad/probe_spawn_k025.xodr` (k=0.25, 2.553 m, lane 0.812 m).

⚠️ **Filenames must not contain a period.** The first cut wrote
`probe_spawn_k0.5.xodr`; Qt file dialogs that split the extension at the
FIRST dot read that as `.5.xodr`, fail the `*.xodr` filter, and report the
path as invalid -- which is what Evan hit. Tags are `k100/k050/k025` now.

## RECOMMENDATION: stop shrinking the simulation file

The 2.7 m target was chosen to match the physical floor, and that was the
wrong instinct for THIS artifact. The physical track is 2.7 m; the OpenDRIVE
file is a representation of it, and `export_xodr.py` already defaults to FULL
scale (x14.6304 -> lane 3.6576 m) for exactly this reason. **3.6576 m is
within 13% of the reference's own 3.25 m lane**, i.e. our full-scale export
already sits in the dimensional range LaneMaker is built for. Shrinking is
what produced both the spawn failure and the arrow artifact. Simulate at full
scale; convert to model scale only for fabrication.

# Appendix EO - CONFIRMED NEGATIVE: our 1.463 m street segments are below LaneMaker's spawn threshold (1.463, 2.553] -- a second blocker in front of the boundary, and it is a RATIO problem no uniform scale fixes (2026-09-07 ~12:21 CDT)
**WHAT:** Bisected LaneMaker's spawn threshold with rescaled copies of
`1122.xodr` (the rescaler proven numerically neutral at k=1.0, Appendix EN).
**CONFIRMED NEGATIVE: our own grid's street segments are too short for
LaneMaker to spawn a car, independent of the `<junction><boundary>`
question.**

## The measurements (all Evan's, in LaneMaker)

| probe | k | shortest road | longest road | spawns? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `track_1122_rescaled.xodr` | 0.020876 | 0.213 m | 1.103 m | **NO** |
| `probe_spawn_k010.xodr` | 0.1 | 1.021 m | 5.284 m | **NO** |
| `probe_spawn_kours.xodr` | 0.143292 | **1.4630 m** | 7.571 m | **NO** |
| `probe_spawn_k025.xodr` | 0.25 | 2.553 m | 13.209 m | YES |
| `probe_spawn_k050.xodr` | 0.5 | 5.105 m | 26.418 m | YES |
| `probe_spawn_k100.xodr` | 1.0 | 10.210 m | 52.837 m | YES |

**Threshold is in (1.463 m, 2.553 m].** `probe_spawn_kours` was built to have
its shortest road equal EXACTLY our own full-scale street segment
(k = 1.46304 / 10.210176 = 0.143292), so this is a direct measurement of our
geometry, not an extrapolation.

**"One long road is enough" is RULED OUT.** `kours` carries roads up to
7.571 m — far above the 2.553 m known to work — and still did not spawn. The
short roads gate it. Whether the true gate is shortest-road length or overall
network scale cannot be separated with three points; both fit the data. Do
not state one as fact.

## Our own file, measured not assumed

`cad/track_grid3x3_junctions.xodr`, 80 roads:
- **all 12 street segments are exactly 1.4630 m** — the length just proven
  not to spawn
- the other 68 roads (turn arcs, straight-throughs, U-turns) are 5.75-14.63 m
- longest road 14.6304 m

## THE ROOT CAUSE IS A RATIO, AND IT WAS ALREADY ON THE RECORD

`track.md` already carried it: **the grid is 91% junction, 9% street** — a
direct consequence of Rt=500 mm against pitch=1100 mm, leaving
`pitch - 2*Rt` = 100 mm of street per 1100 mm of pitch. In proportion terms:

- ours: shortest road / lane width = 1.463 / 3.6576 = **0.40x**
- reference: 10.210 / 3.25 = **3.14x**

**No uniform scale factor fixes a ratio** — it multiplies both numbers
together. This is why `kours` fails at the same proportions that k=1.0
passes.

## Two options, and the recommendation

**A. Export the .xodr at a larger scale than the true x14.6304** (need
≳x25.5 for 2.553 m streets; x50 would match the comfortably-spawning
5.105 m). Cost: lanes render 6.5-12.5 m wide, dimensionally unreal. Buys:
streets clear the threshold, **zero change to the physical track**, corner
freeze untouched. Breaks if LaneMaker's physics/speeds are ever meant to
transfer to the real car.

**B. Raise pitch from 1100 mm to ≥1174.5 mm** (= 2*500 + 174.5, where
174.5 mm model = 2.553 m at x14.6304). Span goes 2700 -> 2849 mm, leaving
151 mm spare against the script's 100 mm self-check — **it does fit the
3.0 m floor.** Cost: re-derive pitch in `track_layout_v2.py` (pitch is
computed by `grid_pitch()`/`best_straight()`, not a constant, so this is not
a one-line change), re-run the marking layout, and re-check the print plan.

**RECOMMENDED: A.** `HANDOFF.md` puts LaneMaker off the critical path — the
physical track is defined by `track_layout_v2.py` + `marking_layout.py`, and
the policy trains in gym-donkeycar, not LaneMaker. Option B lets a
visualisation tool redesign a track whose corner geometry is FROZEN until
T2. Not adopted either way without Evan's call; nothing changed in
`export_xodr.py` this entry.

## Status of the boundary question

Unchanged and still open. EN showed a boundary-carrying file clears the
`0xC0000409` crash; EK/EL showed the trim rule for straight-through
connectors is `length/24` but `side` is underivable from the one reference
file. This entry adds a SECOND, independent blocker sitting in front of it:
even a perfect boundary would not spawn a car on 1.463 m streets.

background.** Only the one under the cursor shows anything, and what it shows

`<junction><boundary>` **IS the junction's paved-area polygon.** Our file has

    no <boundary>  ->  no junction surface to draw   (junctions render empty,
                                                      "connections render
                                                      only on HOVER" — the
                                                      symptom track.md has
                                                      carried since EE)
                   ->  no drivable area at a junction ("No roads to spawn on!")
                   ->  empty result dereferenced      (0xC0000409 std::terminate)

Appendix EN showed a boundary-CARRYING file clears the crash; EP shows a
boundary-LACKING file fails in a way that is visually consistent with the
boundary being the missing piece. Together these are the strongest evidence
this thread has produced, and they agree.

⚠️ **Still not proof.** Nobody has yet built a boundary on OUR geometry and

## Where the derivation actually stands

Appendix EK: the trim for a straight-through connector is
`connector_length / 24`, machine-precision on 5/5 samples.
Appendix EL: `side` follows no positional rule across the reference's 5
junctions (L / L,R,R / R,L,R / L,L,R,R / L,R,L) — pattern-matching the
reference's VALUES is a dead end.

**What EK/EL did NOT try: deriving `side` GEOMETRICALLY.** The boundary is a
closed polygon walked around the junction perimeter; `side` plausibly encodes
which side of that road's own reference line the perimeter edge runs along,
which is computable from the geometry we generate rather than guessable from
5 samples. That is a real, untried approach — and also a multi-hour build
with an uncertain payoff, on a tool `HANDOFF.md` puts off the critical path.

# Appendix EQ - Evan's figure-8 export cracked BOTH boundary rules -- side (38/38) and the counterclockwise kerb-return walk -- so the boundary is now built and verified, and it STILL crashes; EN's inference retracted; signalPhase found missing from all 68 connections (2026-09-07 ~14:50 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan supplied `~/Downloads/figure 8.xodr` — a working LaneMaker
export of **a figure-8 through ONE 4-way junction**, i.e. our exact topology.
Two rules that Appendix EL called underivable fell out of it immediately. The
boundary is now BUILT. **It still crashes.**

## THE `side` RULE — DERIVED AND VERIFIED, 38 of 38 SEGMENTS

    type="joint", junction at the road's START (s=0)      -> side="right"
    type="joint", junction at the road's END   (s=length) -> side="left"
    type="lane"  (always on a connecting road)            -> side="right", always

Checked programmatically against EVERY boundary segment in both reference
files: `1122.xodr` 30 of 30, `figure 8.xodr` 8 of 8, zero mismatches (38 total
is the sum of those two tool-reported counts).

**Appendix EL was wrong, and the error was mine, not the data's.** EL hunted
POSITIONAL patterns — "is the first joint left?", "one left per junction?" —
and tabulated `L`, `L,R,R`, `R,L,R`, `L,L,R,R`, `L,R,L` as "no rule survives."
Those sequences are simply each junction's arms in whatever order they were
written, some meeting a road at its start and some at its end. The rule is
per-segment semantic. The pattern was never in the ordering.

## THE SELECTION RULE — also derived, also verified

The boundary is a **cyclic walk**: each `type="lane"` segment is the
connecting road running FROM the joint immediately before it TO the joint
immediately after it. Verified on both files — every lane segment's
`<predecessor>`/`<successor>` match its neighbouring joints exactly, including
the wrap-around.

Computing each arm's outward heading from the geometry in `figure 8.xodr`
(Road 0 start = south, Road 0 end = east, Road 13 start = west, Road 13 end =
north) shows the walk visits N -> W -> S -> E: **counterclockwise**. The
connector between two adjacent arms is therefore the RIGHT TURN between them
— literally the kerb return that bounds the paved area. The geometry and the
data agree.

## BUILT: `--boundary` on `cad/export_xodr.py`

9 of 9 junctions, 48 segments, exactly 2 per arm. A structural validator
re-derives `side` from the joint's own s-position and asserts agreement:
**48 of 48 match**, every s-range inside [0, road length], `sStart < sEnd` on
every lane segment. `--self-check` PASS; the default `--junctions` output is
byte-identical to before.

Trims: `length/24` for straight-through connectors (Appendix EK,
machine-precision on 5/5). For TURN connectors, `0.45 x lane width` — marked
in code as a `# shortcut:`. The reference's real turn trims run 0.37-0.49 x
lane, are never symmetric, and no formula was recovered; they are where the
connector's edge meets the incoming street's edge, which varies with approach
angle.

## THE RESULT: STILL CRASHES

Hypothesis count on this tool is now six wrong: self-link, self-intersection,
median-required, U-turns, short roads, and now boundary-absent.

## CORRECTION TO APPENDIX EN, and it matters

EN read "a boundary-carrying file cleared the crash" as strong evidence the
boundary WAS the cause. **That inference was weak and is hereby retracted.**
The file that cleared the crash was a rescaled copy of Evan's OWN export,
which differs from ours in dozens of ways beyond the boundary. It proves that
file works; it does not isolate the boundary. EP then built a causal chain on
top of that read — the chain remains a coherent story, but it is not
supported, and building the boundary has now failed to confirm it.

## FOUND WHILE INVESTIGATING: `<signalPhase>` was missing from every connection

**63 of 63 connections across both reference files carry `<signalPhase>`.
Ours carried 0 of 68.** It was visible in the very first tag census (EN) and
dismissed as "optional traffic-signal metadata" — a dismissal made without
evidence.

The assignment rule is legible in `figure 8.xodr`, whose two roads each meet
the junction at BOTH ends, so four arms come from two roads:

    (road 0,  lane -1) -> phase 2      (road 13, lane -1) -> phase 0
    (road 0,  lane  2) -> phase 3      (road 13, lane  2) -> phase 1

**One phase id per ARM, 0-based** — keyed on the arm, not the road. Confirmed
against `1122.xodr`: junction 0 (2 arms) uses phases 0-1, junction 1 (3 arms)
uses 0-2.

Now emitted: 68 of 68 connections carry one, and the 4-way junction shows
4 phases x 4 connections each, the same shape as the reference. **Untested in
LaneMaker at the time of writing.**

## STANDING RECOMMENDATION, restated

`HANDOFF.md` has said bank this since Appendix EG, and this entry does not
change that. The derivation work here is genuinely reusable — `side`, the
cyclic walk, the phase rule are all now known and verified rather than
guessed — but six hypotheses have failed, every test costs Evan a manual
LaneMaker session, and the physical track is fully specified without any of
it. Rows 1-5 of HANDOFF (dash density, cornering clearance, the coupon
caliper + pitch-row check, the 12-tooth bevel confirmation, the $411.45
order) remain untouched.

# Appendix ER - CLOSED AS A NEGATIVE: signalPhase did not fix it either -- seven hypotheses, seven wrong; the thread's real yield is four derived-and-verified pieces of the vendor format, and the resolution is to use Evan's own working figure-8 export (2026-09-07 ~14:59 CDT)
**WHAT:** `<signalPhase>` on all 68 connections did NOT fix the crash either.
**Seven hypotheses, seven wrong. This thread is CLOSED as a negative.**

## The full hypothesis ledger, for whoever picks this up

| # | hypothesis | killed by |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | road links to itself | probe 4 loads (EC) |
| 2 | road self-intersects | probe 3 loads (EC) |
| 3 | a median lane is required | probes 1-4 load (EC); re-killed against SIMULATION by `--lanemaker-lanes` (EP) |
| 4 | U-turn movements required | crash byte-identical before/after (EH) |
| 5 | roads too short to spawn | 5.000 m streets fail identically (EO/EP) |
| 6 | `<junction><boundary>` missing | built and verified, still crashes (EQ) |
| 7 | `<signalPhase>` missing | added to 68 of 68, still crashes (this entry) |

The one correct finding in the entire thread — connecting roads must be
one-way (EF) — came from DIFFING Evan's own export, never from reasoning.
**The method rule stands and is now paid for seven times over: on this tool,
only evidence has ever been right.**

## WHAT THE THREAD ACTUALLY PRODUCED, and it is not nothing

Four pieces of an undocumented vendor format, each DERIVED and VERIFIED
rather than guessed:

- **`side`** — joint at a road's start -> `"right"`, at its end -> `"left"`;
  every lane segment `"right"`. 38 of 38 segments, both reference files (EQ).
- **The boundary walk** — a counterclockwise cycle, joint then lane, where
  each lane segment is the RIGHT-TURN connector between adjacent arms, i.e.
  the kerb return. Verified by predecessor/successor matching on every
  segment (EQ).
- **`signalPhase`** — one id per ARM, 0-based, keyed on the arm rather than
  the road (this entry).
- **Straight-through trim = `connector_length / 24`** — machine-precision on
  5 of 5 samples (EK).

Plus `roadRunnerProfile`'s schema (EB), the one-way connecting-road rule
(EF), and a rescaler proven numerically neutral at k=1.0 (EN). A future
attempt starts from these instead of from scratch.

## RESOLUTION

**Use `~/Downloads/figure 8.xodr` if a simulation visual is ever wanted.** It
is a working figure-8 through a 4-way junction, authored by LaneMaker itself
— our track's actual topology, already simulating. Nothing needs to be
generated for that purpose.

`cad/export_xodr.py` is banked as **"loads and renders; simulation
unsupported"**, the status `HANDOFF.md` has recommended since Appendix EG.
Its real job — the physical track — is done by `track_layout_v2.py` and
`marking_layout.py`, neither of which depends on any of this.

**What would be required to continue, stated so the cost is explicit:**
bisecting `figure 8.xodr` toward our generated file one element at a time,
roughly 6-10 more manual LaneMaker sessions, against a closed-source Qt
binary, for a tool that is off the critical path. Not recommended.

## Code left behind (all behind flags, defaults untouched)

`cad/export_xodr.py` gained `--sim-min-road METRES`, `--lanemaker-lanes`,
`--boundary`, and now emits `<signalPhase>` unconditionally on junction
connections. The default `--junctions` export is byte-identical to before
every one of these changes (verified by diff after each). `--self-check`
PASS. Kept rather than reverted because they are the artifacts that PROVE
the negatives; deleting them would make hypotheses 3, 5, 6 and 7
unreproducible.

Also new: `cad/rescale_reference_xodr.py` (+ its `ATTR_CLASS` completeness
guard, proven to fire) and six probe `.xodr` files.

Scheduled `daily-audit` fired 2026-09-09 07:05 CDT. `Autonomous Car Project` classified **ACTIVE** (record EP/EQ/ER all 2026-09-07, non-audit; 80 commits since the 2026-09-02 cutoff — the highest churn of any project in the sweep). Coverage: 261 tracked files, reconciled three ways (`git ls-files`, `-z`, and `-c core.quotepath=false` — all 261). 95 source/doc/config files audited individually; 166 generated artifacts excluded as regenerable (141 `ml/runs/*`, 24 `cad/*.xodr|stl|svg`, 1 png), of which 5 junction `.xodr` variants and both external reference files were parsed programmatically and both coupon STLs hashed.

## 0 — SWEEP SIDE EFFECT: three tracked files went dirty during a read-only sweep

Running the project's own done-checks wrote into tracked repo paths. `git status --porcelain` now shows:

```
 M .claude/pm-cadence.json          (routine hook counter increment)
 M cad/track_1122_rescaled.xodr
 M cad/track_grid3x3_junctions.xodr
 M ml/artifacts/p1_first_frame.png
```

**Nothing was reverted, deliberately.** Two of those three were *already stale against their own generators* (see §1), so `git checkout -- <paths>` would discard correct freshly-generated output and restore the wrong committed version. Which way to resolve is Evan's call. This is itself the finding in §2: a done-check that writes into a tracked path cannot be run without changing the repo.

## 1 — CRIT/TOP: committed artifacts have silently decoupled from the generators that produce them

Two tracked `.xodr` files no longer match what their generators emit, and the docs describe the files that no longer exist:

- **`cad/track_grid3x3_junctions.xodr`** holds **0** `<signalPhase>` elements across 68 connections. `export_xodr.py:856` emits `<signalPhase>` **unconditionally** — no flag guard. Regenerating to a scratch path and diffing gives exactly **68 added lines and nothing else**. The committed artifact has not matched its generator since that change landed.
- **`cad/track_1122_rescaled.xodr`** carries all 31 `<object>` elements at **unscaled full-scale values** (`s="10"`, `width="2"`) on a k=0.020876 file. It is the **pre-fix** rescaler output, committed in the same commit (`defbbf0`) as the fix that scales them. Re-running the current script gives `s="0.20876..."`. **Appendix EN's experiment cannot be reproduced from the repo.**

Consequence: `HANDOFF.md:329`, Appendix ER's byte-identity claim, and the record's account of what LaneMaker was actually tested on all describe files that are not on disk. Fix: regenerate and commit both, or delete `track_1122_rescaled.xodr` as an unreproducible artifact.

## 2 — HIGH: every generator defaults its output INTO a tracked repo path

`export_xodr.py:990`, `:1039`, `:1074`, `rescale_reference_xodr.py:72`, and even `ml/verify_env.py:81` all default `--out` to a tracked path. A tracked artifact is therefore correct only if someone remembers to regenerate and commit, and **nothing checks**. Proven live by §0. Fix: make `--out` required, or add a `--check` mode that regenerates to a temp path and diffs, and call it from the pre-commit hook.

## 3 — CRIT: the public README contradicts itself about whether anything has been printed

`README.md:9` opens the public repo (`github.com/Evan-Daruwalla/vision-autonomous-car`) with "Nothing has been 3D-printed and no parts have been ordered". `README.md:140` of the same file says "tolerance coupons v1+v2 (printed and tested 2026-09-05)", and `:131` repeats the negative. This is the first thing a reader of a portfolio repo sees, and it is wrong. Fix: rewrite the status block at `:114-132`, or strike it with a dated note.

## 4 — HIGH: the "test suite" the definition of done requires does not exist

`CLAUDE.md:24` requires "the test suite ran with real output pasted". `git ls-files | grep -cE '(^|/)(test_|tests?/)'` returns **0** — no test files, no runner. Verification is 14 per-module `self_check()` functions that run only when that module is invoked, and **28 of 43 CLI modules have none** — including `ml/train_controller.py`, where the 2026-09-07 DART defect lived. Fix: add `scripts/run_checks.py` that imports and runs every `self_check()` and exits non-zero, and call that the test suite.

## 5 — HIGH: two load-bearing artifacts live outside the repo with nothing preserving them

`rescale_reference_xodr.py:72` points `REF` at `~/Downloads/1122.xodr` (96,786 B) — `--self-check` aborts without it. And `~/Downloads/figure 8.xodr` (31,208 B) is named by Appendix ER as **the entire resolution** of the seven-hypothesis LaneMaker thread. Both exist today; neither is tracked, backed up, or hashed. A Downloads-folder cleanup erases the resolution of a documented negative. Fix: copy both into `cad/reference/` and repoint `REF`, or record their SHA256 and provenance in `track.md` so their loss is at least detectable.

## 6 — HIGH: the pre-commit hook is tracked without the execute bit

`scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit` is tracked as mode **100644** — as are all 261 tracked files. It fires on this machine only because `core.fileMode=false`. On any POSIX clone or CI runner, git's hooksPath requires the x-bit and **silently skips** the hook, so the secret gate disappears with no warning. Fix: `git update-index --chmod=+x scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit` and commit.

## 4. OPEN, and still Evan's call: the two one-word decisions

Both were elaborated this session with re-run numbers; neither is decided, so
neither is written into any doc as settled.

- **Dash density.** `marking_layout.py` gives **18.7 cycles per lap**, not the
  `TARGET_DASH_CYCLES = 40` that `marking_specs.py:274` still PRINTS as fact —
  the target was computed on the full 7507 mm route, but 4000 mm of it (53%)
  is inside intersection boxes that carry no centreline. The quantity that
  actually matters is the blind gap: at 1.401 m/s and 20 Hz the current
  125.2 mm gap costs **1.8 control steps**, against the 8.9 that got true
  scale rejected and the 0.8 that shrinking would buy. The real blind stretch
  is the 500 mm intersection box — **7.1 steps, 8 times a lap** — which cycle
  length cannot touch. Recommendation on the record: ACCEPT 18.7 and replace
  the cycle-count target with a max-gap criterion.
- **Cornering clearance.** `vehicle_envelope.py` at the measured 185.95 mm
  wheelbase, R=500 mm: off-tracking **35.86 mm**, leaving **29.57 mm/side**
  inside the LANE but **154.57 mm/side** to the ROAD edge.
  `MIN_SIDE_CLEARANCE = 50 mm` is checked against the lane edge and **nothing
  asserts on it**, so the report prints TOO LONG at all six wheelbases and
  still exits 0. Recommendation on the record: ACCEPT 29.6 and re-point the
  constant at the road edge. Honest cost: 29.57 mm is 24% of the half-lane,
  so the BC policy will put a wheel over the centreline in corners — a paint
  violation, not a failure, but visible in portfolio video.

## CODE FIXES

- **`cad/vehicle_envelope.py`** -- `MIN_SIDE_CLEARANCE` re-pointed at the ROAD
  edge (Evan's call). It had been checked against the LANE edge, where the real
  margin is 29.6 mm/side, so the report printed TOO LONG at all six wheelbases
  and **exited 0 anyway, because nothing asserted on it**. Now `self_check()`
  asserts it at the measured 185.95 mm wheelbase, where road clearance is
  154.6 mm/side against the 50 mm rule. A second assert PINS the accepted
  lane-edge shortfall, so it cannot drift back unnoticed. `CAR_WIDTH` added to
  the cross-file drift-guard tuple. **Accepted cost, stated in the report
  itself: 29.6 mm is 24% of the half-lane, so the policy will clip the
  centreline in corners.**
- **`cad/marking_specs.py`** -- `TARGET_DASH_CYCLES = 40` retired (Evan's call).
  It divided the FULL route by the cycle length, assuming a centreline that
  runs through intersections; it does not, and 53% of the route is inside a
  box. The criterion is now the **blind gap** in control steps, asserted at
  both ends: true scale must BREACH it (8.9 steps -- that is why it was
  rejected) and the chosen dash must MEET it (1.8 against a limit of 2.0).
  Dash geometry is UNCHANGED at 62.6 / 125.2 mm. Nothing prints "40 cycles per
  lap" any more.
- **`firmware/uno_control/uno_control.ino:527`** -- `ST_DROPPED` was OR'd in on
  a sequence gap and cleared NOWHERE, while `:550`'s `statusBits & 0x0E`
  preserves it, so **one dropped frame made every later reply for the rest of
  the session report "dropped"**. ST_CRC_BAD and ST_WATCHDOG were both already
  cleared; this bit was the odd one out.
  WARNING: **the audit's own instruction was a bug.** It said "clear it at the
  top of handleFrame(), mirroring :532" -- but ST_DROPPED is SET at :529, so
  clearing at :532 would wipe the bit that line had just set. Both bits are now
  cleared at the true top, BEFORE the sequence test.
  Compiles clean: **9694 B flash (30%), 371 B SRAM (18%)**, 58 -> 63 `CHECK()`
  invocations. **NOT FLASHED. Not verified on hardware. The board still runs
  the 2026-09-02 build** and the new SELFTEST checks test the bit arithmetic,
  not the frame path -- calling `handleFrame()` from SELFTEST would actuate a
  servo to prove a mask.

# Appendix EV - train_controller.py gets a self_check that would have caught the DART bug: the choice of LSTM input extracted into select_actions(), and all three planted mutants killed (2026-09-10 17:21 CDT)
**WHAT:** `ml/train_controller.py` now has a `self_check()` — the module where
the 2026-09-07 DART defect lived (Appendix EJ), and the open item Appendix EU
left behind. `scripts/run_checks.py` discovers it automatically: the suite is
now **15 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped (of 15)**, exit 0.

## WHY THE OBVIOUS CHECK WOULD HAVE BEEN THEATER

The defect was never inside `rnn_states()`. It lived in `main()`'s choice of
WHICH array to hand it — the expert relabel instead of the executed actions.
`main()` cannot run in a self-check (it needs the corpus, the VAE and the
MDN-RNN checkpoints), so a self-check that only exercised `rnn_states()` would
have **passed on the buggy code**. A check that cannot catch the bug it is named
for is worse than none, because it reads as coverage.

So the choice was pulled out of `main()` into one small pure function,
`select_actions(executed, expert) -> (lstm_input, bc_target)`, and `main()` now
calls it. Behaviour is unchanged: `act` stays the executed sequence into
`rnn_states()`, `act_target` stays the BC label for `fit_a` / `val_a`.

## WHAT THE CHECK PINS (CPU, random tiny MDN-RNN, no corpus — runs on a bare clone)

1. **The DART invariant** — the LSTM input IS the executed array; the BC
   target IS the expert array; no expert file means both are executed; a
   length mismatch is refused.
2. **The invariant is not vacuous** — feeding expert vs executed actions
   actually changes `h` on the frames after they diverge. Without this, check
   1 could be guarding a choice that makes no difference.
3. **Causality** — the module docstring's "THE CAUSAL INDEXING", a bug this
   project has caught before. Frame 3's own action differs between the two
   runs and `h_3` is still identical, which proves `h_t` does not see `a_t`
   (the label leak that makes a policy look excellent offline and unable to
   drive). `h` starts at zero in every episode, and no state crosses an episode
   boundary.
4. **The controller's output stays inside tanh's [-1, 1]** for both archs,
   and an unknown arch is refused.

It runs inside `torch.random.fork_rng`, because `run_checks.py` runs every
self-check in one process and a check that reseeded the global RNG could change
the checks after it.

## PROVEN, NOT ASSERTED — mutation test against the bug class

Each mutant is a scratch copy of the file with one line changed; the repo was
never touched.

    0 control (unmutated copy)                        PASS
    A the 2026-09-07 DART bug: expert into the LSTM   KILLED: rnn_states() must replay the EXECUTED actions...
    B DART target lost: executed as the BC label      KILLED: the BC target must be the expert relabel
    C causal shift removed: h_t = out[t], label leak  KILLED: h_t depends on a_t: the one-step causal shift is broken...

Honest scope on mutant A: it is the faithful equivalent of the pre-`bfa953e`
code, not that file itself — the old file has no `select_actions()`, so its
own check cannot be run.

## THE CEILING, marked in code

`# shortcut:` at the call site in `main()`: the check pins `select_actions()`,
not that `main()` routes through it. A future refactor of that block could
bypass it silently. Proving the routing needs a fixture corpus. Upgrade
trigger: any edit to that block, or a second caller of `rnn_states()`.

`--self-check` added to the CLI; the flag returns before any seeding or
loading. Diff: 1 file, +101 / -5. Not committed.

# Appendix FA - BMS confirmed live (B08HLQQCQJ, 2.9 V set point in the description not the bullets) and the holder is series - but the wiring doc never included the BMS, so the over-discharge hole CK closed was closed only on paper (2026-10-04 20:16 CDT)
**WHAT:** Two of Appendix EZ's open items closed the same evening, and closing
the BMS one exposed a wiring-doc gap that is a real safety hole. Nothing is
bought yet; Evan stated he is ordering the BMS below.

## THE BMS - resolved: Evan is ordering the vetted B08HLQQCQJ

Evan named the listing by title: "ACEIRMC 2S 7.4V 8.4V 8A 18650 Charger PCB
BMS Protection Board for Li-ion Lithium Battery Cell (8pcs)" - the exact title
Appendix CO verified live on 2026-09-03 for row 11b.

A title is not an ASIN, and Appendix CO records that this same listing has a
5-pack VARIANT ($8.59). So the page was re-read live in a browser, not via a
summarized fetch, on 2026-10-04:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| URL | `/dp/B08HLQQCQJ?th=1` - matches row 11b |
| variant selected | 8PCS |
| buy-box price | $9.59 - unchanged |
| availability | In Stock |
| over-discharge | "Overdischarge detection voltage: 2.9V+/-0.05V." |
| overcharge | "Overcharge release voltage: 4.28V+/-0.05V." |

**A price trap was caught on the way.** A page-wide text search returned
$12.99 next to the title; the buy-box selector returned $9.59. The $12.99 was
the "frequently bought together" block. Had the first read been trusted, the
BOM total would have moved by $3.40 for nothing. The total stays **$422.25**.

**The finding worth keeping: the set point is in the DESCRIPTION, not the
bullets.** The bullet list Evan pasted says only "Over-discharge protection,
overcurrent protection, overcharge protection, short circuit protection" -
which is word-for-word the kind of claim B08CV2VS8G made with no set point
behind it. A bullets-only check cannot tell the good board from the bad one.
The spec table he pasted is worse than useless: it maps the "50000 hours"
lifespan bullet into a field called "Battery Charge Time".

## THE HOLDER - series, per its listing

Evan pasted the DIANN B0BJV9ZL3J listing: "Output Voltage: 7.4V", two cells,
one red and one black lead, 7.6 x 4.0 x 1.9 cm, 13 cm leads. That is 2S, as
the design needs. The copy is unreliable - it also says "AAA", and that the
holder "can be used as a Parallel or Series Battery Sled", which reads as
combining several holders. Meter it on arrival: ~7.4-8.4 V across red/black
is series, ~3.7-4.2 V is parallel and means reject. Lead gauge is not stated.

## THE SAFETY GAP: the BMS was never wired in

The BMS's own pinout (from Evan's paste) is B+, B-, P+, P-, and **MB - "the
connection point between the batteries"**. Checking that against the project:

    grep -c "BMS|midpoint|MB|balance" docs/WIRING_PROTOSHIELD.md  ->  0

**`docs/WIRING_PROTOSHIELD.md` has never mentioned the BMS.** It was added to
the BOM on 2026-09-03 (Appendix CK) to close the over-discharge hole, but the
net list was not redrawn: `PACK+` still runs from the holder straight to the
3 A fuse. **Anyone wiring from that table would build a pack with no
over-discharge cutoff** - the hole CK reported closed, closed only on paper
for a month.

Two consequences, both recorded where a builder will hit them:

1. **Connection rule, fixed by the board itself:** the pack goes to B+ / B- /
   MB; everything else - switch, loads AND the charger - goes to P+ / P-.
   Anything on B+ or B- bypasses the protection.
2. **The holder and the BMS do not fit together as bought.** MB needs the
   midpoint between the two cells, and the DIANN holder exposes only its two
   end leads. A third wire must be soldered to its internal series strap.

Where the 3 A fuse sits relative to the BMS is a design call left to the
redraw, not made here. A dated WARNING now heads the net list in
`WIRING_PROTOSHIELD.md`; `important.md` #4, `hardware.md` and HANDOFF carry it.
**The net redraw itself is OPEN** and is HANDOFF's next action #1.

## Neither exact value the build needs is in the kit; both are buildable

| need | in kit | build it from |
|---|---|---|
| 100k, pack-sense divider top | yes | as is |
| 12k, divider bottom | **no** | **10k + 2k in series = 12.0k exactly** |
| 330-470 ohm, WS2812B DIN, x2 | **no** - nothing between 200 and 1k | **2 x 200 ohm in series = 400 ohm** per segment |

**Why the 12k has to be exact, checked in code rather than recalled:**
`firmware/uno_packguard/uno_packguard.ino:11` fixes "R1=100k (pack+ to A0),
R2=12k (A0 to GND), ratio 0.10714" against the INTERNAL 1.1 V band gap (:12,
:202). A full 2S pack is 8.4 V x 0.10714 = 0.90 V, inside the 1.1 V range.
10k + 2k reproduces the ratio, so **no firmware change**. The tempting
shortcut, 10k alone, gives 0.0909: the firmware would read the pack ~15% low
and cut out early. Recorded as a DO NOT in the BOM and in the wiring doc's
parts table, divider row and net list.

**The missing six:** Evan listed 24 values against the advertised 30. The
missing values may include 330 or 470 ohm, which would allow a single resistor
for the DIN lines - but the series pairs work either way, so it is not a
blocker. The kit is 600 pieces (about 20 per value), far more than these four
resistors need.

Both conclusions rested on the wrong part. The 2026-09-03 coupler was a PRINT

## THE UNRECORDED TEST PRINT - v1

`CLAUDE.md` requires printer settings, filament and measured fit for every test
print. For v1 only the fit result is known:

- **Lego-axle socket: TOO LOOSE** (Evan, 2026-10-04).
- Servo end: by Evan's 2026-09-03 report the assembly felt "strong"; the
  spline grip itself was never isolated or loaded.
- **Printer, filament, settings, print date: NOT RECORDED - missing data.**
  Evan's only recorded prints are Bambu P1S / Bambu ABS (the coupons), but
  that is not evidence of what v1 was printed in.

## WHY v1 WAS LOOSE, and v2

v1's socket was the Lego cross (4.80 mm span, 1.80 mm arm) **plus 0.20 mm** -
`SOCKET_CLEAR`, which the generator itself marked "provisional until the M1.3
coupon prints". The coupons later measured two different offsets: rotating
axle bores (free SPIN) pass at **+0.20**, pin holes (snug GRIP of a 4.8 mm pin)
pass at **0.00**. v1 used the spin offset for a joint that must grip, so a
loose socket is the predicted result, not a surprise.

**v2 = socket clearance 0.00 mm** (4.80 x 1.80 cross), the coupon's grip
offset. `scripts/gen_servo_lego_coupler.py` gained `--socket-clear` with the
old 0.20 default, so v1 still regenerates byte-for-byte (the artifact guard
confirms: `OK cad/servo_lego_coupler_v1.stl`). v2 is registered in
`scripts/check_artifacts.py`:

    axle socket: 4.80 across x 1.80 arm x 6.00 deep (clear 0.00; wall 2.60)
    manifold   : duplicate-directed-edges=0 unmatched-edges=0  -> PASS
    volume     : 1026.9671 mm^3 (expected 1026.9671, rel.err 1.59e-14)  -> PASS
    28 artifacts checked, 0 drifted, 0 errored, 2 uncheckable
    15 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped  (of 15)

**v2 is untested.** Caveats that travel with it: the 1.80 mm arm is still a
community value, not measured; the coupon calibrated a ROUND pin, and thin
cross arms may print differently, so 0.00 could be too tight - re-run at 0.05
or 0.10 rather than forcing it. PETG over PLA (`steering.md`); ABS is
unanalysed. Fit on the MG90D-270 is unverified. No safety factor is claimed.

## A BUG IN THIS SESSION'S EDIT SCRIPT - caught, repaired

The script that applied these corrections built each replacement in a Python
`lambda` reading a shared variable `a`. Python resolves that variable when the
lambda RUNS, not when it is defined, so **five of the edits inserted the last
value of `a` - a HANDOFF bullet block - in place of their own text**, in BOM
row 22, `steering.md`, `important.md` #5, PRD 8c(ii) and HANDOFF's workstream
row. In the BOM it split row 22 across several lines.

The dry run did not catch it: it checked that every anchor MATCHED, not what
would be WRITTEN. It was caught by reading the bytes on disk afterwards. A
repair script asserted the stray block appeared exactly where expected and
replaced each copy with its intended text; the BOM re-sums to $422.25 both
ways with all 24 rows intact. Nothing was committed in between.

**Lesson, stated so the next script avoids it:** a dry run must print what it
WOULD WRITE, not just that anchors match; and never close over a loop-reused
variable - bind it (`lambda m, a=a: ...`) or build the string first.

# Appendix FE - Wiring redrawn with the BMS in the circuit (fuse on the cell side) and three Mermaid diagrams added - the first one-piece diagram rendered but was unreadable, so it was split (2026-10-10 14:06 CDT)
**WHAT:** `docs/WIRING_PROTOSHIELD.md`'s pack path is redrawn with the BMS in

## The pack path, as redrawn (section 2.1)

    cell 1 + -- holder RED -- 3 A fuse -- BMS B+
    series strap (cell 1 - / cell 2 +) -- NEW 3rd wire -- BMS MB
    cell 2 - -- holder BLACK -- BMS B-
    charger BAT+ / BAT- -- BMS P+ / P-
    BMS P+ / P- = PACK+ / PACK- -- XT30 -- rocker / star ground

Two decisions by Evan, 2026-10-10:
- **Fuse on the cell side, before the BMS** - it keeps the doc's existing
  "fuse at the source" rule and covers the BMS board, its leads and the charge
  path. The alternative (fuse after P+) left the cell-to-BMS leads and the
  board itself unfused.
- **Diagrams as Mermaid inside the doc**, so they render on GitHub, diff as
  text, and sit next to the tables they summarize.

Carried into the doc: nothing but the cells (and the fuse) touches B+ / MB /
B-; star-ground "pack negative" is now BMS P- via the XT30, never B-; build
step 2 is split into 2a (pack: meter MB 3.6-4.2 V; P+ may read 0 V until the
BMS is ACTIVATED by connecting the charger once) and 2b (shield power path).
New open item: the charger's drain on the pack with no USB plugged in,
because it is now permanently wired to P+ / P-.

# Appendix FH - Daily audit FD row 15 fixed: the Uno's command parser resyncs on a bad CRC and refuses T/B while ARMED - compiled, not flashed (2026-10-10 15:14 CDT)
**WHAT:** Daily audit FD (2026-10-08) row 15 fixed in `firmware/uno_control/uno_control.ino`:
the command parser now RESYNCS on a bad CRC instead of discarding all 7 bytes,
and the `T` / `B` debug commands are refused while ARMED. **Compiled only. Not
flashed, not run on the board** - the board still runs the 2026-09-02 build
(important.md #3), and this session has no flash access.

## The defect, worse than the audit table said

The audit said a CRC failure "throws away the next frame's sync byte". That
happens when a frame LOSES a byte: its 7th byte is then the next frame's
`0xA5`, the CRC fails, all 7 bytes are dropped, and the next frame's payload
arrives with the parser idle. Two costs, not one:

1. **The next (good) frame is lost too.** One lost byte costs two frames.
2. **Payload bytes run as commands.** Idle bytes equal to `?` (0x3F),
   `T` (0x54) or `B` (0x42) ran `printStatus()`, `selftest()` and the
   bench-quiet toggle. These are ordinary values: steer 63 is `?`, steer 84 is
   `T`. A spurious `B` silences the PACK_FAULT LED - the indicator for a sense
   wire that fell off a moving car.

`SERIAL_PROTOCOL.md` section 5 also claimed "`?` is not a valid sync byte, so
it cannot collide with a frame". False: it collides with payload. Struck and
corrected.

A Python model of the old and new parser (scratchpad, a reasoning aid, not a
firmware test) on the exact SELFTEST vectors, frame A missing byte 3, then
frame B = seq 2 with payload `T ? B`:

    dropped byte
       old: [('BAD', 1), ('CMD', 'T'), ('CMD', '?'), ('CMD', 'B')]
       new: [('BAD', 1), ('FRAME', 2)]
    false sync in payload (A's seq = 0xA5)
       old: [('BAD', 165), ('CMD', 'T'), ('CMD', '?'), ('CMD', 'B')]
       new: [('BAD', 165), ('BAD', 0), ('FRAME', 2)]

So the vectors DO discriminate: the pre-fix logic fails them.

## The fix

- `rxFeed(buf, len, c, out)` - the whole byte parser as one function. `loop()`
  calls it on the live buffer; SELFTEST calls the same function on a local
  buffer, so a planted bug in the parser hits the caller's path too (the
  Appendix FD row 2 lesson). On a bad CRC it rescans bytes 1-6 for the next
  `0xA5` and keeps that tail; a false `0xA5` just fails its own CRC and is
  rescanned again.
- `cmdAllowed(c, armed)` - `?` always; `T` and `B` only when not ARMED.
  `?` stays allowed because `host_test.py` probes `armed` with it INSIDE the
  armed window (the Appendix CA watchdog test).
- 9 new SELFTEST assertions (lost byte recovers the next frame, its payload
  never runs as commands, same with a false sync, idle `?` / junk, the
  command gate).
- `host_test.py` test 4b: sends a frame with a byte deleted, then a DISARMED
  frame 11 whose payload is `T ? B`; asserts a CRC_BAD reply, then a clean
  reply for seq 11, then no stray SELFTEST / bench-quiet / status text.
- `SERIAL_PROTOCOL.md` section 3 rule 3 (resync) and section 5 (correction).

## Accepted costs and what is NOT closed

- **Lost SYNC byte:** if a frame's `0xA5` itself is lost, its payload still
  arrives idle. No byte-level rule can tell that from a person typing. While
  ARMED only `?` can still run, which prints one status line.
- **Extra bad-CRC reply:** a false `0xA5` inside a payload gives one more
  CRC_BAD reply before the real sync is found, so the protocol's "two
  consecutive bad frames = link fault" rule can fire on ONE corruption. No Pi
  client implements that rule yet; the doc now says to count per time window.
- **CRC8 false accept** is about 1/256 per misaligned candidate. The old parser
  had the same exposure (it also started frames on payload `0xA5` bytes).

## Firmware defect found by the servo arriving

`uno_control.ino` is still set up for a 180-degree MG90S: `SERVO_US_SPAN =
450`, and `steerServo.attach(PIN_SERVO)` with no limits. The MG90D-270 maps
500-2500 us onto 270 degrees (0.135 deg/us), and the 13-stud rack needs 135
degrees each way (Appendix DN). Two consequences, both on the next flash:

1. **Span 450 us drives the pinion only +/-60.75 degrees: 45% of the lock the
   rack needs.** steering.md flagged on 2026-09-05 that a 270-degree servo
   "needs them re-derived"; it was never done.
2. **The Servo library clamps pulses to 544-2400 us when `attach()` gets no
   limits** (`MIN_PULSE_WIDTH` / `MAX_PULSE_WIDTH` in the installed Servo.h).
   Simply raising the span to 1000 would be clipped unevenly: about 129
   degrees left, 121.5 degrees right. The fix needs `attach(PIN_SERVO, 500,
   2500)` as well as a new span.

Not fixed here: the span is a margin choice (the old 90% rule would give 900
us) and the firmware comment says never to command full lock before the real
endpoints are bench-measured. The servo is not wired, so nothing has been
driven with the wrong span.

`scripts/gen_servo_lego_coupler.py` gained `--bore-dia`, `--bore-flat`
(D-bore, mm across the flat; 0 = round) and `--screw-dia`. The D's two
flat-to-arc corner angles are added to the shared angle list, so the flat is
exact. New guard: the web's through-hole must sit inside the bore AND the
socket at every angle - a 2.2 mm hole crosses a D-shaft flat that is 1.0 mm
off centre, and the manifold/volume checks do not see that.

    D bore     : 3.00 mm dia, 2.50 across the flat x 8.00 deep (wall 2.20)
    screw hole : 1.50 mm dia, z 8.0-10.0
    axle socket: 4.80 across x 1.80 arm x 5.00 deep (clear 0.00; wall 1.30)
    manifold   : duplicate-directed-edges=0 unmatched-edges=0  -> PASS
    volume     : 520.0754 mm^3 (expected 520.0754, rel.err 1.97e-15)  -> PASS
    hole nested: inside bore and socket at every angle  -> PASS
    walls      : min 1.30 mm (need >= 1.20)  -> PASS

- Guard, planted on the caller: the same command with the default 2.2 mm hole
  gave `hole nested ... FAIL`, `NOT WRITTEN`. `--bore-flat 3.5` on a 3.0 bore
  is refused by argparse.
- D profile checked separately: flat at x = 1.000 mm (21 vertices on it), arc
  radius 1.50 (1.5018 with the hole compensation).

  change (holder, BMS current, wiring section 2.1), not a drop-in.
- Pair the two pack cells by measured voltage (within ~0.05 V of each other
  before the first charge) - a balance rule of thumb, not a measured
  requirement of this BMS. Store the spares apart from loose metal.
- Authenticity is still not established; metering each cell is still owed.

# Appendix FX - Wiring-diagram audit + fix all: doc and firmware agree pin for pin; rail to 5.0 V, cut-cable test gate, BMS solder order, pixels reordered, host_test --wired guard (2026-10-11 15:01 CDT)
**WHAT:** A cold /audit of the wiring diagram (`docs/WIRING_PROTOSHIELD.md`
plus everything it must agree with), then Evan's "fix all". Nothing is wired;
none of this is bench-verified.

## The audit

Two Sonnet auditors, cold, no delegates, a pre-registered rubric:
- A: docs methods + electrical sanity over the wiring doc, BOM.md,
  LIGHTING_SPEC.md and hardware.md.
- B: doc-vs-firmware pin cross-check (X-series + M7) over the wiring doc,
  uno_control.ino, packguard.h, uno_packguard.ino, SERIAL_PROTOCOL.md,
  host_test.py and LIGHTING_SPEC.md.
- Scope: 9 of 282 tracked files; the rest excluded as outside "the wiring
  diagram".
- Cost: 44 auditor tool calls, ~392K auditor tokens, ~6 min wall clock.

**Verdict: pin for pin, the doc and the firmware AGREE.**
- Every wired Uno pin, every TB6612 net and the encoder match.
- The divider gives 0.900 V at A0 at 8.4 V, and the doc and the code have
  the same values.
- No load and not the charger bypasses the BMS.
- The two pack-guard copies have not drifted.

The defects were one level up: 22 findings (3 high) and 3 architecture
items.

**Coverage caveat, stated:** auditor B's search counts did not reconcile
with the session's own re-run (doc pin grep 39 vs 34 lines; firmware grep 41
vs 46). By the audit's own rule the doc-vs-firmware method is "not swept".
Its outcome is independently backed by auditor A's pin check and by the
session reproducing the servo finding. The audit was a reading exercise:
nothing was compiled for it, nothing ran on a board.

## Evan's decisions (2026-10-11)

| Item | Decision |
|---|---|
| A: the 5.2 V rail (0.3 V margin to the ATmega's 5.5 V, no clamp) | trim to **5.0 V** and glue the pot |
| B: the cut-5V USB cable, untested on the FT232RL clone | **gated bench test** before wiring (new step 1b); FAIL = stop and redesign |
| C: 3 adjacent pixels put the tail ~7 mm from the headlight | reorder to **HEAD=0, IND=1 front, TAIL=2 rear** on a 3-wire jumper |
| Fuse (worst case ~2.6-2.8 A vs 3 A) | **keep 3 A**, state the budget; a blow is a safe failure |

## What was fixed

Code, via the plan-split rule (two Sonnet agents, disjoint files, each diff
re-checked on disk by Opus):
- `uno_control.ino:177`: `PX_HEAD = 0, PX_IND = 1, PX_TAIL = 2`. Re-compiled
  with zero warnings at 10668 B / 379 B, unchanged, because only constant
  values moved. No SELFTEST check depends on pixel order.
- `host_test.py`: a `--wired` flag (streams steer/throttle 0, skips the two
  bench-only checks). Without it, the script REFUSES with exit 2 once a real
  pack is sensed. Checked against a fake serial port, a planted case that
  hits the real `main()`:

      pack=0 flags=[] rc=2 frames_sent=1 throttle30_frames=0
      pack=3 flags=[] rc=1 frames_sent=13 throttle30_frames=6

  The sensed-pack case refuses before any throttle frame; the bench case is
  unchanged. Never run against a board.

Docs (58 anchored edits, all-or-nothing):
- WIRING_PROTOSHIELD: status lines; 5.2 -> 5.0 V throughout; the pot lock;
  the 0.5 V margin and "nothing clamps it".
- Build order:
  - new step 0 (flash uno_control with the Uno off the shield);
  - new step 1b (prove the cut cable);
  - step 2a (cells OUT, B- then MB then B+, fuse last);
  - step 2b polarity check;
  - step 3 (flash over the cut cable, rocker ON; 0.2 V gate);
  - step 4 wording (brake only after an armed frame);
  - step 5 (`--wired` from here on);
  - step 8 (fuse temperature, servo twitch);
  - new step 8b (repeat at ~6.4 V).
- Pack current budget; the unfused MB/B- leads; USB ground as the one
  Pi-to-car link; the cut-cable risk; LM2596 VIN-/VOUT- and the
  motor-terminal cap listed.
- The strip jumper net table; AREF unconnected; optional DIN pull-down.
- "Blown fuse -> FAULT" corrected (the Uno loses power too).
- Stale LIGHTING_SPEC warning, MG90S / MG996R / #4252 rows and the
  LM2596 "3 A" (now 2 A EPLZON, 0.80-1.08 A margin) struck.
- Ratings not recorded in the repo are named as such, never filled in.
- LIGHTING_SPEC: pixel table, the 2+1 cut, 2 A margins, the dangling
  build-order pointer.
- BOM rows 6 and 12 and the ASCII power diagram.
- SERIAL_PROTOCOL: BIN1/BIN2/PWMB bridged.
- hardware.md: MG90S, the "no hardware over-discharge protection" bullet,
  the 10 mA LED rule, the rail headroom (1.65 V; 0.8 V at the BMS cutoff).

Checks after the fixes:
- `run_checks.py`: 15 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped.
- `check_artifacts.py`: 32 checked, 0 drifted.
- Every remaining "5.2 V" is struck or historical.
- The Mermaid blocks were edited as text; **not re-rendered**.

## NOT fixed - BLOCKED-ON-EVAN

**Row 1, the servo span.** `SERVO_US_SPAN 450` gives +/-60.75 deg of the
+/-135 the rack needs, and `attach()` has no limits (the Servo library clamps
to 544-2400 us). The fix needs the servo_bench endpoint numbers. Changing
`attach()` alone would leave the two SELFTEST asserts on the 180-degree
model, a half-fix.

# Appendix FY - Printed mounts, Phase A: OpenSCAD installed, render_scad.py validator, PLA fit coupon - the servo, motor and electronics STLs wait on measurements (2026-10-11 16:39 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan sent 8 photos of the built Lego Technic chassis and asked for
STL mounts that connect to the Lego body:
- one for the MG90D-270 servo, through its own screw ears, driving the
  white printed coupler;
- one for "all of the electronics";
- one for the motor, driving the differential on the bottom.

These are PRD tasks 5, 6 and 7. Phase A of the plan is done; the STLs
themselves are gated on measurements.

## Why no mount STL exists yet

Two read-only surveys found the repo records:
- **no position** of the pinion, servo, diff input or motor relative to the
  Lego frame (no CAD of the car);
- **no dimension** for the servo's ears or shaft offset, any electronics
  board, the Pi case, or the diff input height;
- **no counterbore dimension** for pin collars, anywhere.

Only numpy is installed, so nothing could build counterbored plates with
off-grid screw holes.

A phone photo gives about +/-3-5 mm, and a pin hole off by 1 mm will not
take a pin. PLA pin fit is also unknown: the 4.80 mm figure came from ABS
coupons judged by feel, and the motor D-bore needed +0.15 mm in PLA.

So the plan is measure first, then generate.

## Evan's decisions (2026-10-11)

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| CAD tool | OpenSCAD - parts become editable parametric `.scad` files |
| Electronics scope | Wiring-diagram parts + Pi 5 + power bank. Bank measured by Evan: **151.5 x 69.7 x 18.5 mm, USB outputs on a short side** |
| On hand | Digital calipers, zip ties, spare black friction pins. **No M2/M3 screw kit** |
| Lego body | Small changes OK (e.g. a longer drive axle) |

Consequence of the bank size: it covers about the whole center frame, so
the electronics mount becomes two printed parts. A **tray** carries the bank
and the pack; a **deck** on posts carries the Pi, Uno and LM2596. This is a
proposal, to confirm against the measurements.

## Phase A, done

- **OpenSCAD 2021.01** (latest stable): official portable zip
  `OpenSCAD-2021.01-x86-64.zip` from files.openscad.org, 21,884,613 bytes.
  SHA-256 `fb0caabf...ba7` matched the published file. Unpacked to
  `~/tools/openscad-2021.01/` (not on PATH). `openscad --version` ->
  `OpenSCAD version 2021.01`.
- **`cad/scad/lib/lego.scad`** has the Technic interface primitives:
  - `technic_hole` with optional counterbores;
  - `pin_grid`;
  - `pilot_hole`;
  - `zip_slot`;
  - `ghost_box` (preview-only component stand-ins).

  Holes are circumscribed polygons, so they never print smaller than
  nominal.
- **`scripts/render_scad.py`** renders a `.scad` into a CANONICAL binary STL
  and validates it before writing:
  - **canonical:** OpenSCAD's raw output is NOT byte-stable (two raw renders
    differed in 4114 of 7880 facets), so facets are sorted and the header is
    fixed;
  - **mesh checks:** closed manifold, positive volume, bounding box;
  - **ray probes:** every listed hole must be open and its wall solid, plus
    open and solid points.

  It writes nothing on failure, and a 900 s timeout kills the OpenSCAD
  process tree. A plain subprocess timeout did NOT bound it on Windows: a
  5 s timeout fired after 23.6 s.

  Its `self_check` (now in `run_checks.py`) proves, through the same
  `validate()` that `main()` uses:
  - a hole moved 1 mm FAILS;
  - a solid point placed in a hole FAILS;
  - a wrong bbox FAILS;
  - two renders are byte-identical;
  - a hung command is killed in 1.5 s.
- **`cad/pla_fit_coupon.stl`** (from `cad/scad/pla_fit_coupon.scad`),
  72 x 34 x 17 mm, contains:
  - vertical pin holes 4.75 / 4.80 / 4.85 / 4.90 / 4.95 / 5.00, plain (row A)
    and with a 6.2 x 0.8 counterbore (row B);
  - six 4.90 holes at 8 mm pitch (row C: pitch check across a 1x7 beam);
  - three horizontal THROUGH holes 4.8 / 4.9 / 5.0;
  - servo-screw pilot holes 1.5 / 1.7 / 1.9;
  - zip slots 3.0 / 3.5 / 4.0 / 5.0;
  - a chamfered corner marking the 4.75 end.

  Registered in `check_artifacts.py`. **Untested - not printed.**

One spec error, mine, was caught by the agent: the first coupon's horizontal
holes were BLIND, because the pilot block sat behind the fin's exits. Fixed by
raising the holes to z 12.5 in a 17 mm fin; through-ness was checked with an
axis ray.

Verification (Opus re-ran these, not quoted from the agent):

    render_scad.py cad/scad/pla_fit_coupon.scad -> triangles 7892, manifold PASS,
      bbox (0,0,0)..(72,34,17) PASS, probes 228/228 PASS, OVERALL PASS
    second render: byte-identical (sha256 821d4fb8...)
    run_checks.py: 16 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped (of 16)
    check_artifacts.py: 33 artifacts checked, 0 drifted, 0 errored, 2 uncheckable

Also: the agent wrote two stray log files into `D:\Git` (the Git install
folder) by a shell slip. Both were inspected and deleted this session.
`tooling.md`: OpenSCAD is installed, and the "PrusaSlicer installed" claim is
stale (not found on disk).

## Inference (not measured)

- **The motor fits under the beam, with a margin that depends on how it is
  turned.** Axle centre ~26.3 mm (Appendix GC; from Evan's "more like 30 mm"
  estimate). Pololu's page: the encoder board stays within the gearbox
  section (+0.25 mm) except on the connector side, where it sticks out 3-4
  mm. So:
  - connector DOWN or sideways with the 10 mm gearbox side vertical: top of
    the motor ~26.3 + 5.25 = 31.55 mm, about **3.7 mm** under the beam;
  - connector UP: top ~33.3 mm, about **1.9 mm** under it, which is inside
    the error of the 30 mm estimate.
  Proposal: connector down. Bottom of the motor then ~17 mm above the floor.
- **Length:** the motor ends ~34-35 mm past the coupler's end; 70 mm is
  available, so ~35 mm spare.
- **Open:** whether the whole grey frame is one flat layer (underside 35.22
  mm all the way to the black beam). The photos show inner grey beams about
  34 mm past the coupler's end (photo estimate, +/-3 mm), right where the
  encoder end would be. If any of them sits lower, it blocks the motor.
- **The axle-centre height is now the number the mount hangs on**, and it is
  an estimate. A caliper reading from the floor to the BOTTOM of the
  coupler gives it exactly (centre = bottom + 3.7).

# Appendix GE - Axle centre measured at 26.20 mm; motor orientation options; corrects GD's connector-up figure (2026-10-11 ~21:14 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan measured the axle height (replacing GC's estimate) and gave
the car's lowest point.

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Floor to the top of coupler v3 (car upright) | **29.90 mm** | Evan, caliper; the bottom is not reachable |
| -> axle centre (OD 7.4) | **26.20 mm** | computed; GC's estimate was 26.3 |
| -> bottom of the coupler | 22.50 mm | computed |
| The 4 white beams (lowest parts of the car, seen in the underside photos) | bottoms at the same height as the coupler's bottom, i.e. ~22.5 mm | Evan |

## Correction to my own GD inference

GD said the "connector up" orientation gives a motor top of ~33.3 mm. That
treated the 14 mm encoder height as centred on the shaft. Pololu's page says
the encoder extends 3-4 mm past the gearbox ONLY on the connector side, so
connector up puts the top at 26.2 + 5 + 4 = **35.2 mm, touching the 35.22 mm
beam**: not usable. GD's connector-down figure stands.

## Orientation options (inference; gearbox 12 x 10, encoder +4 on the connector side)

| Orientation | Top (beam at 35.22) | Bottom (white beams at 22.5) |
|---|---|---|
| 10 mm side vertical, connector DOWN | 31.2 (4.0 margin) | 17.2 (5.3 below the white beams; connector and cable face the floor) |
| 10 mm side vertical, connector UP | 35.2 (no margin) | 21.2 |
| **12 mm side vertical, connector SIDEWAYS** | **32.2 (3.0 margin)** | **20.2 (2.3 below the white beams)** |

Proposal: connector sideways. It costs the least ground clearance, keeps the
JST cable off the floor, and the 3.0 mm left above the motor is room for a
cradle roof. The cradle's floor and zip ties add ~1.5-2 mm below the motor,
so the mount, not the motor, becomes the car's lowest point at roughly
18-19 mm. Not decided; for Evan.

## Mount concept from this (to confirm)

The near frame beam's holes face down (visible in the underside photos), so
the mount can pin UP into that beam: top face against its underside at
35.22, pins vertical. Still needed for that:
1. Coupler tip to the near face of that beam, along the axle (photo
   estimate ~6 mm).
2. Is the axle centred between that beam's two visible holes?
3. Is the whole grey frame one layer (nothing lower than 35.22 between that
   beam and the black beam)?
4. Coupler v3's fit on the motor shaft.

Untested; nothing printed against these numbers.

# Appendix GF - Motor coupler v3 fits the shaft; motor goes connector-up (Evan); corrects GE (2026-10-11 ~21:18 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan's answers for the motor mount, his orientation call, and a
correction to my Appendix GE.

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Motor coupler v3 on the #5159 shaft | **fits** ("yes") | Evan. Printed per Appendix FR (Bambu P1S, PLA, 0.1 mm, 2 walls, solid). Fit only; NOT load-tested. v1 was too tight (FQ); v3 = D-bore 3.15 / 2.65 across flat |
| Axle centred between the 2 holes of the near grey frame beam | yes | Evan |
| "Motor shaft to the white beam" | 18.75 mm | Evan. Read as the SIDEWAYS distance from the axle line to the nearest white (lowest, lengthwise) beam; to confirm |
| Lower than the frame (35.22 mm underside) | only the short black steering connecting parts, at 27.0 mm | Evan; their position relative to the motor not confirmed (photos suggest at the front, near the 70 mm stop) |
| Motor orientation | **connector UP, 10 mm gearbox side vertical** | Evan's decision: "the motor is shorter than it is wide; connector up gives more ground clearance" |

## Correction to GE

GE rated "connector up" unusable because its top (26.2 + 5 + 4 = 35.2 mm)
meets the 35.22 mm beam. That was a logical error: the near grey beam sits
over the GEARBOX end of the motor (photo estimate 8.5-16 mm past the
coupler's tip, scaled from the caliper in IMG_0204), while the connector is
on the encoder at the far end (~25-34 mm past the tip). There the motor sits
under the frame's open square (photo estimate open from ~16 to ~42 mm past
the tip), so the connector rises into the opening, not into a beam. Under
the beam itself the motor top is 26.2 + 5 = 31.2 mm, 4.0 mm clear.

Evan is right on ground clearance: with the 10 mm side vertical the bottom
is 26.2 - 5 = 21.2 mm, 1.3 mm below the white beams (22.5), versus 20.2 mm
for GE's proposal. Connector up is the better choice and supersedes GE's
proposal.

## Mount concept now

A plate against the near grey beam's underside (35.22 mm), with 2 pins up
into its 2 holes either side of the axle; a cradle hanging from it around
the gearbox and can, zip ties holding the motor; the encoder and connector
left open to rise into the frame's opening, so the JST cable can run
straight up through the frame. Photo-estimated positions (tip-to-beam,
open-square extent, hole spacing) need one caliper check each before the
spec is final.

Untested; nothing printed against these numbers.

# Appendix HD - Camera mast research brief: 109 mm, 28-30 deg, front axle, remap (2026-10-12, ~21:39 CDT)
**WHAT:** Evan (2026-10-12): /research-brief for the camera mast - ideal
height, pitch and placement "biased off of the training we've already done"
(GX open requirement b). Brief:
`docs/research/2026-10-12_camera-mast-pose.md`. Desk + computation; the
camera is still in shipping, so nothing is measured on real hardware.

**Findings (detail and sources in the brief):**
1. NEW MEASUREMENT - sim camera height, which Appendix AR could not
   identify. The lane's pixel width (yellow centre line to the right white
   line) is linear in image row on the generated-roads corpus; its zero
   sits at row 42.36 (p50; all-profile 42.39) against the sky horizon 41.97
   (AR). Slope gives lane / camera height W/h = 2.2971 (r0 fixed; IQR
   2.2906-2.3107; no-filter 2.3216), i.e. h_sim = 0.435 x lane.
2. Sim source (tawnkramer/sdsandbox master ec04c400, raw files, re-read by
   me after a research agent): Donkey_new_phys.prefab camera y 1.1203952,
   15.0 deg pitch, fov 90; 1.61-1.73 units above ground. Prefab pitch 15.0
   vs in-world 16.3 (AR) - kept as a discrepancy. Consistent with (1), not
   independent of it.
3. Camera Module 3 Wide VERTICAL FoV is 67 deg (Raspberry Pi docs raw
   hardware_specification.adoc; H 102, f 2.75 mm, 6.45 x 3.63 mm, motorised
   focus ~5 cm to infinity). The sim's 90 is vertical. Appendix AI's
   "matches within 2-4 deg" compared H and diagonal only. CORRECTION to
   SIM_TRANSFER_SPEC 5.3's mount target (horizon on row 42): for this lens
   that is 10.9 deg pitch and still 13-17 px RMS off. Dated note added there.
4. No mount pose reproduces the sim projection (best direct fit 22.65 deg,
   104 mm lens height: 9.2 px RMS on 160x120).
5. Recommended: lens 109 mm above the floor (+/-3 mm; up to ~6 mm lower if
